ST. RE LENS PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION. 1885. FELLOW FLECTORB,—The Conservatives have now formally announced to you "that Colonel Gamble commands their sin- cere respect, and that egoism him personally they have no- thing to say." We, therefore, make this final appeal to you with the utmost confidence. ' Everybody agrees that the personal composition of the new House of Commons Is a matter of very grave importance. Too many of its members are sure to look upon it as a mere club ; still more will only regard it as a stepping-stone to same we isolated appointment ; and Color el Gamble, we need hardly point out, belongs to neither of these cissees He has, oit the other hand, been willing to work quietly In the awe, nmeet of local affairs (charitable. educttional, and municipal) for many years ; mud, now, when a e have our first opportunity of conferring a public honour, we cannot, in com• mon fairness, pass such a worker by. Apart from these considerations. Colonel Gamble is, in our opinion, the besS representative St. Helens etn possibly have. He knows both the past history and the present wants of all our industries. He works dto take the tax off corn ; and is now anakllB to see everything untaxed that comes upon our tables, and so to re-adjust taxation generally that It shall fall, In fair propor- tions, on the shoulders best able to bear it. He b-lonas to the Party that ~cured the abolition of the Glass and Window Duties, and so set free the G ass Ti ode; and that took off the Salt Tax, and so made possible our large hernical Works. These, in.their turn, are the Industries which, both here and throughout the country, largely consti- tute the Coal Market ; the freedom o which Colonel Gamble is anxious, if possible, still further to prom.te by the abolition of the London Coal Dues. . Our Candidate is, moreover, personally pledged to Reforms in the land and Labour Laws, in the Laws affecting the Regis.' tratiou of Voters, and in the Procedure of the House of Corn- mons. While he does not "in season and out of season" parade the fact, he is, nevertheless, a staunch supporter of Religion and Religious Education in their fullest sense; and, although he sees no objsetion to abolishing School Fees in ad Elementary Schools, be is supremely resolved to preserve and strengthen the existing Denominational System. . To those who wquld ask yeu to believe other wise, you may point with confidence to Colonel Gamble's past conduct and the characters of the men who are supp rting him. As to Irelann, which, thanks to the late Liberal Govern- ment, wit be more fairly represented in the next House of , Commons than it has ever been before, Colonel Gamble is pre- pared to respond to every reasonable and intelligent demand which their representatives may make. A man of the views we have just referred to, who Is also a successful business man and an experienced worker on public boards, is, we again submit, just the retnesentative that a busy town like ours requires in a House of Commons with practical work before it. As to his opp ment, we will only say this; to whatever ex- tent he is properly claimed to be a Laneashire or tit Helens Man. to that same extent, with reference to his ancestral. div.head: (g,ottrg.
div.p: (g,ottrg.

AN AUTUMN SONG. In Spring we hope; in Summer we possess; In Autumn we remember, and confess • 'That what was ours, is ours for evermore; Lost to our eyes, but added to our store. For Beauty, passing over open hearts, Enters, abides, and never more departs. So vanished sunshine, wind, and shower we see, In the grand form of every sheltering tree ; Gladly received, and freely given again, The growth of summer's joy, and winter's pain. 0 Memory, thy ripened sweetness charms More that young Hope, with eager, outstreteched arms! The path is thickly strewn with faded flowers, That would not blossom in these earthly bowers; But, in their midst, nourished by their decay, Life budded, blossomed, and bears fruit to-day. And if stern Winter tor awhilo hide all, Sweet memory tells us 'tis no funeral pall; So well we know his face, his sombre mood No longer frights us; for he does not brood O'er slumbering Beauty, till she rises, fair As ever, and the richer for his care. What know we of the Future? 'tis the Past Which bids us hope all will be well at last. Thus far we have been led through paths unknown, Guided and kept, by wisdom not our own. We think we know the hand; and sometimes trace, But oftener have to trust, the unseen grace ;1 And memory bids us be content to wait, And trust our Father, not blind, ruthless Fate. Though bright hopes fade away, yet He will give. Beyond our hope, all that We need to live A life far higher than our loftiest dreams, Deeper and fuller than the myriad streams Of Art and Nature, that have nourished man Since his long history on earth began; While Memory owns, with ever widening store, That what was ours, is ours for evermore! SArATAIRS WRIGITT, in The Sunday at Home.

div.p: Tlvrittio.

" Mamma," said a little boy, who bad been sent to dry a towel before a. fire, "is it done when it's brown? It was said of Sir Robert Peel—" He is the horsiest man on foot and the footiest man on a horse I ever saw." A gentleman in the country advertises for a tutor to teach latin to Geiser, and Groek to Xenophon; also math- cmatics to boys under 16. Money will make us work, but money will not make us give OUT hearts to the work—nothing but love for our work or real good principle can make us do that. Better a dinner of verbs where love is than a whole banquet of nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, prepo- sitions, and conjunctive conjunctions with hatred therein. Tommy don't like fat meat. One day the stake was fat. "Tommy," asked the professor, " will you have some beefstake?" "Yes, sir; but I dent want any that has pork all round it." A little girl who had often heard her mother speak of her father, who was somewhat bald, as being a selfmade man, asked her one day, if her father was a selfmade man, why he did'nt put more hair on his head. We are all frail, but do thou esteem none more frail than thyself. Had we no faults of our own, we should not take so much pleasure to note them in others. Never ,compare thyself with others, unless it be to advance them and depress thyself. The highest and most profit- able lesson is the true knowledge and lowly esteem of -ourselves. Stop and think.—lf thou can'st not continually' recol- lect thyself, yet do it sometimes, at the least oncea day, namely, in the morning or at night. In the morning fix -thy good purpose, and at night examine thyself what thou hest done, how thou hest behaved thyself in word, deed, and thought, for in these perhaps thou hest often- times offended against God and thy. neighbour. The war song of the Zulus runs—g Turn! Turn I Yuan! Turn! Yum ! Turn! Turn! Yum ! Yuan! Turn! Turn! Turn! When they want to vary the monotony they sing it backwards. When Isaiah Thomas, the printer of Massachuseets, was printing his almanack for the year 1780, one of his boys asked him what he should put opposite the 13th of July. Mr. Thomas being engaged, replied. "Anything, anything!" The boy returned to the office, and set, -" Rain, hail, and snow." The country was all amaze- ment when the day arrived, for it actually rained, hailed, and snowed violently. From that time Thomas's almanac was in great demand. A certain Turkish pasha's visit to the Bank ofXngland was the occasion of a curious raisunderstandieg. The governor of the bank placed a small bundle of bank-notes in the hand of the pasha, remarking that it represented a million pounds sterling. Ibrahim realm, thinking it a complimentary gift, proceeded to pocket the notes, and they had the greatest difficulty in convincing him that the notes had been placed in his hand merely as a curi- -osity and not as a gift, when reluctantly, and with a -crestfallen mien, he restored them to the governor. OVER Fnesn.—" I intended to tell Jane to bring a fresh bucket ot water," said the wife of Professor Not- tlehead, looking up from her sewing. "You doubtless mean a bucket of fresh water," rejoined her husband. "I wish you would pay some little attention to rhetoric; your mistakes are embarrassing." I few moments later the professor said, "My dear, that picture would show to better advantage if you were to hang it over the clock." "Ah !" she replied, "you doubtless mean if I were to hang it above the clock. If I were' to hang it ever the clock we couldn't tell what time it is. I wish you would pay some little attention to rhetoric; your mistakes are embarrassing." Gnus FIRST.—" The best husband I ever met," says a living writer, "came out of a family where the mother, a most heroic and self-denying woman, laid down the absolute law, ' Girls first'—not in any authority but first to be thought of as to protection and tenderness. Conse- quently, the chivalrous care which these lads were taught to show to their own sisters naturally extended itself to all women. They grow up true gentlemen— gentlemen generous, unexacting, courteous of speech, and kind of heart. In them was the protecting strength of maahood, which scorns to use its strength except for protection; the proud honesty of manhood, which infi- nitely prefers being lovingly and openly resisted to being " twisted round one's finger.' as mean men are twisted, • and mean women will always be found ready to do, but which I think all honest men and brave women would not merely dislike, but utterly despise." JUVENILE Ceixe.—Of the influence of pernicious liter- ature in making criminals, Mr. Devitt says, in his re- cently-published "Leaves from a Prison Diary ": ° Among young thieves are often foundouths who have had honest parents and a proper bringing up. These are the victims of such works as Blueskin," Three-finger Jack," Jack Sheppard," Claude Duval,' 'Dick Turpin,' and the various other pestiferous criminal novelettes which have obtained such an immense circulation among boys of the industrial classes of these countries during the past twenty years. The writers of these thief-making sheets represent their pickpocket, burglar, or highway- plan hero in picturesque colours, and hundreds of bright, intelligent boys have been torn from the homes of re- spectable parents through they instrumentality of this literature of rascaldom, and have become cast, in most -eases for their whole future, among the felon ranks of habitual criminal life." Prince Peter, of Oldenburg, is chief of the Imperial Colleges for Girls, and exercises the duties of the office with diligence. Lately he decided to investigate for him- self whether there were grounds for the numerous com- plaints which had reached him of the food at the Smol- nig Convent, where eight hundred girls were educated, Going, to the institute just before diriner, he walked straight to the kitchen. At the door he met two soldiers carrying a huge steaming cauldron. "Halt!" he cried out; "put that kettle down." Thel soldiers obeyed. "Bring me a spoon," continued the Prince. The spoon was produced, but one of the soldiers ventitred to begin a stammering remonstrance. "Hold your tongue," said the Prince; "take off the lid; I insist on tasting it." No further objection was raised, and his Highness took a large spoonful. "You call this soup?" he ex- claimed; "why, it is dirty water !" "It is your High- ness," replied the soldier; "we have just been cleaning out the laundry." MurnEns AND SONS. —Fathers must be content to Stand second to mothers, It is the mother who has to teach the babe to Inovv the father, and slowly to frame its unused lips to speak his name. The father is the first stranger the child grows familiar with, hut the mother never was a stranger—the infant first widens its fresh eves by fixedly gazing on her face. There is no face in all the world which a man ever knows so well—not even hers with whom, at a far later day, he stands before the altar, and who thenceforward shares his name. The gentle sadness of this theme only comes fully out when you remember that, in the course of things, a time arrives when that most familiar of countenances is seen wider a change. Mothers grow aged, it may be infirm, while sons progressively tower up into the prime/of life. Then the early attitude of this closest related pair on earth is touchingly altered. She who in the first period gave all help has now to lean on the grown figure which she once so lightly dandled as a child, now standing before her strong and straight as the father did in the long gone days. God has given to men no sweeter, dearer, richer feeling than a grown son has when repay- mg to an aged mother a little tithe of the loving care she early lavished upon him. In this relationship of mother and son God has made sure that every rough male heart shall have a tender spot—one sacred recollection. And whenever it dawns upon the mind that it was He who gave the loving mother, joy for that most bountiful of all bestowals draws the son of the earthly mother towards the Father who is in heaven.

Little Arthur had been to church. On his return, his sister asked him how he liked the sermon. "Well," implied the youthful critic, "the beginning was very , good, and so was the end, but oh! there was a great deal I too much middle !" Use no stratagems and devices to get praise. Some inquire into the faults of their own actions or discourses on purpose to hear that it was well done or spoken, and without fault. Others bring the matter into talk, or thrust themselves into company, and intimate and give occasion to be thought or spoken of. These men make a bait to persuade themselves to swallow the hook, till by drinking the waters of vanity theyswell and burst. Front tells a story that well illustrates Turner's cha- racter. Turner, Prout, and Varley had been together on a sketching tour in Devonshire. They had to cross a ferry; Varley had not at the moment a sixpence in his pocket, so he borrowed one from Turner. The next morning Prout and Varley left Exeter to return to Lon- don. Although the coach started at six o'clock on a very cold morning, to their surprise, but greatly to their satisfaction, they saw Turner at the coach office waiting to see them off. "Ah !" said Varley, "this is really very kind of you. Turner, to be up so early to bid us goodbye !" "Oh," said Turner, "It isn't that; but you forgot to pay me back the sixpence you borrowed from me yesterday !" LAVE INDEPENDENT OF RENOWN. —Nowoman will love a man better for being renowned or prominent Though he be first among men, she will be prouder, not fonder; as is often the case, she will not even be proud. But give her love, appreciation, kindness, and there is no sacrifice she would not make tor his content and comfort. The man who loves her well is her hero and king. No less a hero to her though he is not to any other; no less a king though his only kingdom is heart and home. It is a man's own fault if he is unhappy with his wife in nine cases out of ten. It is a very exceptional woman who will not be all she can to an attentive hus- band, and a very exceptional one who will not be very disagreeable if she finds herself wilfully neglected. THE FIRST LAW OF CRILDHOOD.—The first law of childhood, to be followed as rigorously es it is inculcated, is that of absolute obedience to authority. This is a necessary condition for safety, not to speak of peace. Where children do not obey orders or attend to prohibi- tions they are always in some danger. From the rotton branch of the tree up which they are told not to climb, and up which they forthwith swarm, to the reading of a forbidden book—from the treacherous morass which they are warned not to cross alone to the undesirable acquain- tance whom they are urged to drop and forbidden to bring home—it is the same thing. Age and experience know—youth and ignorance do not; and the only safety for youth is to be guided by the better wisdom of age in those things where experimentalising is dangerous and a mistake is a disaster. A COURAGEOUS BISHOP.—The following story is vouched for by the Rev. J. L. Jackson :—" George IV., soon after Dr. Sumner was made Bishop of Winchester, sent to him to say that he intended to receive the Holy Communion. By some mistake the Bishop arrived half an hour later than the King expected, which irritated his Majesty ex- tremely, and on the arrival of the Bishop he found him • in a state of mind which he judged quite unfit for such an ordinance. After hearing with the greatest respect and humility the King's expressions of anger at the • delay, which were in one instance accompanied by an oath, the Bishop expressed the greatest sorrow for the unfortunate mistake, but firmly, though couched in the • most respectful language, refused to administer the Sac- rament to him whilst his mind was in its present agitated state. At first this only enraged his Majesty still more, but the Bishop remained steady to his resolve, and left the palace. In a week the King sent for Sumner • again, shook hands with him and thanked him for his previous refusal, and requested, if he then thought it proper, that he might receive the Sacrament from his hands."—The Journal of Nary Frampton. THE Porr BOWLES.—He was in the habit of riding daily through a country turnpike-gate, and one day he presented as usual his twopence to the gatekeeper. "What is that for, sir ?" he asked. "For my horse, of course." "But, sir, you have no horse." "Dear me !" exclaimed the astonished poet, "am I walking, ?"—Mrs. • Moore relates that Bowles on one occasion gave her a ' Bible as a birthday present. She asked him to write her , name in it. He did so, inscribing the sacred volume to her as a gift—" From the Author."—The following story • comes from a gentleman farmer, one of Bowles's , parishioners, who cherished an affectionate remembrance of the good parson. One day there was a dinner party at the parsonage. The guests and the dinner were both kept waiting by the non-appearance of the host. At last his wife went upstairs to see what mischief had delayed him. She found him in a terrible "taking," hunting:every- where for a silk stocking that he could not find. After due and careful search, Mrs. Bowles at last discovered the reason of the "loss." He had put both stockings on one leg. CURE FOR DISTIONESTY.—The Saracen's Head Hotel, Lincoln, was noted for three things—a very gruff land- lord, a very cheeky waiter, and "365," the latter term being a synonym for the very best rice pudding I, or anyone else, ever tasted; and as it was produced every day in the year, we christened it "365" I can vouch for it being on the table twice a month tor 22 years, and always good alike. I may add that if half-a-dozen were required, they were always forthcoming. But it is of Arthur, the waiter, I would speak. It Was often sus- pected that this swallow-tailed, modest-looking garcon was guilty of removing the decanters, and especially the small black bottles of crusty, " bee's-wingy old port, before they were quite empty; this was especially noticed by a Mr. Thompson, a sharp-witted "commercial," who, on the day in question, hinted the fact to the president. It was a rather large dinner party, and Arthur was in unusually good form. A pint of old port was ordered, and emptied; the bottle was partly refilled with salt, pepper, cayenne, mustard, Worcester sauce, Chili vine- gar, anchovy, &c. "Bring in the bill, Arthur," said the president. "Yes, sir," and, as usual, Arthur hurriedly took off the black bottle. The company waited some time, but no Arthur and no bill appeared. Whereupon the " vice " was asked to ring the bell. In came "but- tons.' "Tell Arthur to bring in the dinner bill at once," said the president. "Please, sir, he can't, he's nearly dead; he's choked." The gentlemen at the table became alarmed, hurried out of the room to find poor Arthur in a most painful position. He was black in the face, and was surrounded by his fellow-servants. On his recovery, he solemnly promised never again to test the quality of leavings in the black bottle.—The Ambassadorslof Com- merce. By A. P. Allen.

Boss Pinar TRINS.—The time to plant all kinds of fruit trees has been already dealt with, and we will now explain how to plant bush fruit trees. If we watch a novice planting a tree,tie is certain to make a deep per- pendicular hole, its depth corresponding with the length of thei robts :t. the plant he is about to deposit in it. Dawn into this the toots are thrust in a huddled condi- tion, quite unlike the position they occupied when taken up. It is not the nature of roots to descend in that man- ner; they travel laterally, and to ;whatever depth they descend it is done gradually by a few only, the majority keeping near the surface, within the influence of the source of light and heat. The holes for bush fruits should not be more than ein. deep and slightly convexed, .and their width should be sufficient to allow the roots to be spread out evenly all ' over the surface. In order to maintain the plant in an upright position, hold it with one hand whilst the other is engaged with the spade in placing some of the finest and best soil next to the roots, and the coarser material nearer the surface. To a depth of 61n. the soil should be all good or it will not grow fruit, but when the top two or three inches are sweet and friable it will be at all times more acceptable to the roots. Each tree will require to be slightly pressed with the foot all round over its roots, but the surface should be left loose all round. Young plants should haye three or four shoots on a clean stem; that is, one free from growth or side shoots. The stem may be from 6in. to 12in. long, and if furnished with any shoots they should be moved by cutting close up to the stem, but the prun- ing or shortening of the shoots must be deferred till spring, after nearly an inch of growth is made. Of gooseberries, the following are useful sorts for general use and profit, and those who wish to exhibit must choose exhibition sorts :—Reds: Crown Bob is a free bearer and of good flavour. Black Prince is a fine dark free bearing sort. Ironmonger is an excellent flavoured one. Red Champagne is very sweet; and Warrington is a very late variety, and good in every way.—Whites: Whitesmith, free and fine flavour; so is Early White and White Champagne. Early Sulphur and Yellow Ch3.rn- pagne have yellow skins, and aro excellent sorts. Of Currants, the Black Naples is best of the blacks. Reds: Raby Castle has large bunches and berries. Red Dutch and Knights, large red, are good sorts.llChampagne, a pink coloured skin variety, and the White Dutch, are all useful in their way, especially for those who exhibit col- lections of hardy fruits. Raspberries should be repre- sented by either Carter's Prolific or Prinee of Wales. Mr. Raymel, of Penworthans, has one called The Queen, but such a name does not appear in the catalogues. We therefore conclude from its handsome appearance that it is one of the above. There is no comparison between the sorts usually grown in gardens and the sorts referred to, and we would earnestly direct cultivators' attention to them.

THE FRONT GARoxx.--Gladioli, where there is doubt of their standing out of doors uninjured, should be taken up without cutting the tops down, and tied up two or three together, and suspended from the roof of a building such as an outside shed or wash-house where there is not sufficient heat and moisture to excite them. Some that we are acquainted with that were left in the ground last season flowered much later than those that were lifted, and otherwise cared for. Dahlias may be .it down and dug up, and if dry at the time they may remain exposed for a few hours, or they may be taken under cover where plenty of air can get at them to dry them well before they are stored away for the Tinter. Any position will do to winter them that is not too warm and dry, or too moist and not frost proof. If it is found that some varieties are liable to go off in winter:whilst others remain sound and plump, they should be tried in boxes covered over with thoroughly dry sand or ashes. I Some recommend sawdust, but this is apt to encourage fungus growth if it gets the least damp, and for that reason should be avoided. TRH WlNDOW.—Tuberose Begonias are now grown in most gardens, and when their culture becomespbetter understood they will find their way to cottage windows. They have flowered well in a sunny position !outside during the past season. Those in pots will now require less water, but at no time must they be allowed to get dust dry. They would keep well in a box as advised for Dahlias, only the ashes or sand that covers them need not be so dry DS recommended for Dahlias,

Thee was a wife's troubled heart and a son's saddened spirit in the home at Clay Cues, Derbyshire. when, in the autumn of 1884, it was mournfully whispered by man to man, and from neighbour Is neighbour, that the One-3 robust and healthy Joteph Beresford had been given over to die. Whea for more than forty years one has lived as boy and man near the place of his birth, his neighbours are the most competent judges and beet witnesses touching his merits as a man of sin- cerity and truth. Thus long has Mr. Joseph Berestord lived among she pe,ple of that village, and is vouched for by al his neighbours as an Intelligent, reliable, and popular citizen. For many years he had been, and still is, a deputy manager of the coal-mining business of that place, Ur. Berestord's late physi- cal prostration was but another striking instance, among many constantly coming to public knowledge far beyond their immediate locality, how loternal maladies suddenis and mys- teriously develop, and the most robust of men, in the prime of life, are called to suffer the most painful affliction even nuto the verge et the grave. Until this nom/lion Mr. Berestord had rarely If ever known a day of Ulnas,. The alternatioue from perspiring heat several hundred yards in the bowel, of the earth to the chi ling blasts ,d winter winds on the surface, added to office duties and the anxieties incident to his trust, added to the safety aud welfare of his me-a, are doubtless among the principal caused to which may be attributable his ultimate physical prostrapon.

r. Be'reaferd's first oonsciousness of bodily derangement was a pain in his side. aocompanied with sickly faintness, fol- lowed very soon by what seemed an enlargement of the liver, as it was apparent to external observation, eausing muck pato and distress when he lay upon either side in bed, as th ugh it adhered to the inner surface of his body. In tie autumn of 1884 he was compelled to resig , his duties and retire from his employment, saying he could stand it no longer. Then his stomach gave way—faintness, a sensation of all-gonenees, watery mouth, nauseousness, loss of appetite—food taken would sooner or later be thrown up, undigested as when taken, and the once-powerful man became but s shadow et his former self. As he was daily and hourly growing weaker, his doctors frankly and honestly expressed their inability to do for him any in 're. and as their last advice recommended him to try hydropathic treatment at a near establishment. This advice he followed, and took the hydropathic course for several weeks. but finally discovering no signs of relief for the alarming all- mente of his stomach and liver, and still growing pi,orer and weaker, he abandoned all hope of living, and went hornets die, saying to himself It was uowise to waste more money on hie poor body; that if he had anything left after being placed wader the sod his good wife had better have it. Mr. , Beresfsrd'm history from this time is best related in one of his neat and explicit business letters, condensed as a tele- gram : " Leaviog the water cure establishment," he writes, "I was a very little better, but very week, because I could not; eat anything to co me any good. for my stomach couldn ot digest food, and my liver was as bad as ever. It is known to all my friends and neighbours what a poor creature I was. I had given myself up as an incurable—bad ceased to take medicine, and only waited the end, feeling that death would be a happy relief. Some weeks later it was suggested by a good neigh- bour and life-long friend—in fact he insisted—that I should try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I was very loth to-de se, as t had had many shillings' worth of ail sorts of medicine, and all to no purpose. It was like throwing money away. However. I was not only physlcally but mentally too weak to resist the positive mind and earnest entreaty of my friend, to which were jelned the solicitations of my wife and son. A small bottle of the medicine was procured, and I took it. I cannot say that I felt any specially good effects from it, but I was so very low that I had no right to expect much impr ivement from one little bottle. When It was gone aeother bottle appeared which took the same course under the directions, and before it was quite all gone I had al- most quite forgotten to think about my unhappy stomach. Food began to relish and act on my stomach as in former days. To my happy surprise, and to the delight of my family. I found myself improving. I then made up my mind I would sttok well to the Syrup. I did so until I had taken nine bottles. when I was ones more a well-man. I got to work again after being off about five months. loan truly say that lam cured of indigestion and liver troubles. I had for weeks abandoned all doctors' pre criptiona or o'her medicines before I began with Selgel's Syrup. Since about March (l 884 I have not taken regularly any of the Syrup, but only occasionally when I find myself getting a little out of order by reason of exposure to very damper chilly weather. I then take a few drops, and ft puts me right again at once. " Since I have tested the value'of the medicine in mv own case I have recommended it he many people, and have given some of myown away for a test, as it is said, ' The proof of the pudding is in the eating, thereof.'" Mr. Beresferd relates with much pleasant humour the ex- pressions of utter astonishment of his business acquaintances at finding him at his old place again. "What on earth cured you ?" he says, is the question asked him almost daily. Even one of his good doctors—who, he says, is his warm personal friend, and still his 'amity physician—was wont to ask the wife, " What did fi,ally cure Joseph?" When she modestly replied, "Mother Belgel's Syrup."

RECOVERY OF SUNKEN TREASuRE.—In February last a Spanish mail steamer named Alfonse XII., belonging to the Lopez line, from Cadiz to Havana, sank off Point Grand°. Canary, in 25i fathoms depth of water, and about a mile from the shore. She had on board treasure valued at £lOO.OOO. The underwriters who had insured this treasure organised a salvage expedition, which was despatched to the scene of the wreck in May last under the superinten- dence of Captain Stephens. On Monday morning a telegram was received from that gentleman as follows : Lambert has got both scuttles open, and into the magazine. The boxes of gold are there. Lambert is there." ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- ✓ P CULTVRA &o. ' A valuable lot of Jersey heifers have been sliuma ironi the Island of Jersey by Mr. E. J. Arnold for breed- ing purposes in Belgium. The Jersey herd of Colonel H. S. Russell was recently sold at New York, when sixty-one cattle realised an average of over £5O, and a total of over £3,135. Frefich agriculturists, in investigating the nutritive qualities of forage stored in silos, have diseovered that clover's° kept is more conducive to the increase of weight in animals than fresh clover. Mr. E. J. Arnold, of Summerland, Jersey, shipped re- cently twelve fine gray Jersey heifers, selected from the best Island herds, for France. They are to increase the valuable Jersey herd of Comte Lariboisiere. Ensilage is making steady progress in this country in 'spite of prevailing depression. The agricultural returns ' for 1885 show that there were at the time of enumera- I tien 1,181 silos in Great Britain, art compared with 610 in 1884. The Royal Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural So- ciety has agreed to offer £l5O in prizes for Welsh stock at the society's show next year, and the Welsh Cattle So- ciety has started a subscription list with a view to raising a similar amount The Shorthorn bull Bright Andrew (49186) sold at Mr. Pugh's sale to Mr. Naylor, has been resold to Mr. James How, of Broughton. This is a very handsome bull, heavily fleshed, with nice coat of hair, and he has already himself a valuable sire in Mr. Pugh's herd. At the recent sale of Jersey cattle, the property of Mrs. Shoemaker, of Burnside Park, Baltimore, U.S.A., some long prices were realised. One cow made £650, another £220, and another £2OO, other prices ranging from £BO down to £33, whilst £350 was given for a bull and £6OO for a bull calf. Mr. Horsfall, Limefield House, Burnley, has recently sold to Mr. Richard Botterill, Tathwell Hall, Louth, at a long figure, a magnificent yearling Oxford bull of choice Duchess and Oxford blood, being by the noted sire Vis- count Oxford 4th (44209), who is also sire of Lord Fitz- hardinge's 1,150-guinea heifer at Mr. Holford's sale. , From American advices we learn that tho Messrs. Cos- grove, of Le Suer, Mimi, had their show herd of fourteen head of Herefords destroyed by fire on the railway. The Fears containing the cattle were next to the engine, and the straw took fire from sparks. Besides the cattle lost, two of the attendants were seriously injured. HEIFER DIFFICULT TO MILL—It is stated in an Ameri- can paper that a hard-milking cow may be managed as follows :—Make of some whalebone or ivory a long, thin plug for each teat, larger in the middle to prevent it slipping outtand with a head of sufficient size to pre- vent it slipping in. Make the plugs very smooth, and after greasing them with glycerine and sweet oil mixed, insert them in the teats, and keep them in the ducts, ex- cept when milking. In a short time the passage will be permanently enlarged. During the quarter ended September 26 there were 2,803 fresh outbreaks of swine fever reported in Great Britain, and 11,986 swine were attacked, of which 3,128, or more than one-fourth, died. In the preceding quarter the outbreaks amounted to 3,188, and there were 15,407 swine attacked. Under the operation of the England Markets and Fairs (Swine Fever) Temporary Order, the disease has declined, and this order has been continued to the end of the present month, as previously noted. • LORD AMMON AND TES ALLOTMENT SYSTEL—Some correspondence has taken place this week between Mr. Wedmore, a working man, who has been lecturing in Dor- set on the allotment system and Lord Alington. In a letter dated from the Jockey Club, Newmarket, Lord Alington says:—" I shall be very glad to see you, and, what is more, be very much obliged if you can sketch out some plan—small holdings or allotments—which I could carry out to benefit the working man. It is a very difficult subject; but as you know the me ci well, you might be able to tell me what they want, and what would be of substantial use to them. I want to see the labourer a free and happy citizen of a free and happy country. He is not so at this moment." Mr. Wedmore, writing in re- ply, under date Nov. 2nd, says Labourers must have their cottages independent of the farmer or employer, as until that is done the labourer cannot be free, as he can- not sell his labour in the best market and get full value for it, and he must have as much land as he and his family can cultivate properly at the same price as it is let to the farmer, and when any industrious, persevering man can get sufficient capital to take 10, 20, or 30 acres, let him have them." , SPLENIC Farsa.-.-Splenic fever affects different ani- mals, is not confined to any particular climate or lati- tude, although more prevalent in some localities than others, and appears in districts without the movement of diseased animals. When introduced into fresh dis- tricts, usually retains its vitality, and reappears at un- certain intervals. No partial immunity to any animals known, and all affected animals seem capable of trans- mitting the poison. The blood and tissues contain a virus which certainly produces disease in a man and animals by inoculation. The carcases of diseased animals most dangerous and probably one off the prin- cipal means of spreading the disease. No general ex- tension of disease occurs among animals which are taken into splenic fever districts, as in the ease of Texas fever, and no period of time is sufficient to acclimatise animals or confer immunity from attacks of splenic fever. Period of incubation extremely short. No:well-defined symptoms observed. Animals usually die very sud- denly. Enlargement of spleen, with great increase of weight. Hemorrhagic patches on serus and mucous membranes without ulceration. Presence of the Bacil- lus antharasis in the blood and spleen after death. ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY OF ENGLAND.—The monthly Council was held on Wednesday week. Pre- sent—His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, K.G. (president, in the chair), Earl Cathcart, Earl of Coventry, Earl of Feversham, General Vicount 'Bridport, the Hon. E. K. W. Coke, Sir A. K. Macdonald, Bart., Sir Massey Lopes, Bart., M.P., Mr. W. Gilbey, Mr. J. Howard, M.P., Col. Kingscote, C. 8., Mr. T. H. Miller, Mr. Jacob Wilson, Dr. J. A. Voelcker, and Professor Brown. Col. Bingscote, C.B. (chairman), presented the report, from which it appeared that the Secretary's receipts during the past three months had been duly examined by the Committee, and by Messrs. Quilter, Ball, and Co., the society's ac- countants, and found correct. The balance in the hands of the bankers on October 31st was £4,354 17s. id.; and £2,000 remained on deposit. The quarterly, statement of subscriptions and arrears to September 30th, and the quarterly cash account, were laid on the table; the arrears then amounted to £2,028. The Committee recommended that the names of 33 members, whose addresses cannot be ascertained, and others who, from various causes, are unable to pay, be struck off the list of members. The Committee recommended, in order to carry out the wish of the judges of farms in Class 3 (Preston), that a silver medal be awarded to the eldest daughter of Mr. T. Fearnall.—This report was adopted. TETE SHIRE-HORSE Socurry.—A well-attended meeting of the Council of this Society was held on the 3rd inst. Mr. Wm. Wells (president) in the chair. Mr. Walter Gilbev reported that the secretary's receipts had been examined by the committee, and found correct, that the balance at the society's bankers was £1,004 ss. 2d., and that the committee recommend the investment of a fur- ther sum of £5OO in Government stocks, making the in- -vested capital £2,000. Various payments, amounting to £2ll is., were recommended to be paid. The Horse Show Committee recommended the payment toPir. 0. M. Sexton of the balance of commission on the auction sale at the last show. It was recommended that a gold medal (the weight not to be less than 2 oz.) be given to Ithe breeder of the champion mare at the next London show; also that all champion cups to be given by the society, except the " Elsenham challenge cup," which will be accompanied with a gold medal, the gift of the donor of the cup. That the prizes offered for competi- tion in classes 1, 2,3, 4, and 5, be first prize £2O, second prize £l5, third prize £lO, fourth prize £5, instead of the three prizes in these five classes as formerly, and thus increasing the prizes in these five classes by £5O. A cor- dial vote of thanks was tendered to Mr. T. H. Miller for the presentation to the society of an oil painting of " Honest Tom" (1,105). It was carried unanimously that a champion prize of £25 be offered to the council of the Royal Agricultural Society for the best Shire stallion in the Norwich showyard.

THREATENING AN M.P.—Mr. R. Richardson Gardner, M.P. for Windsor, has received an anonymous letter, threat- ening to shoot him should he attend any more political meetings at the theatre. Mr. Gardner promptly offered a reward of £5O for any information which will lead to the conviction of the writer of the letter.

SANKEY V. RUNCORN OLD BOYS (2ND Tnadus).—Played at Sankey on Saturday, the home team being defeated by one goal and two minor points to nil. Sr. HZLENS v. Sr. HELENS HECRBATON.—These claim played their first matcn this season on the St. Helens ground, which was in capital condition. The gtme was very evenly contested, and ended after an exciting finish in favour of St. Helens by one goal and one minor to St. Helens Recreation one try and two minors. WARRINIPTON 2ND V. WARRINGTON ROVERS. This match was played on Saturday on the Rovers ground at Bewsey, IR the presepce of a large number of spectators. Considerable local interest prevailed in consequence of the Rovers having won every match this season. Warrington, however, proved the winners by 2 tries and 5 minors, to nil. _

SANKHY V. RUNCORN OLD BOYS (Isv Timis).—The Sankey Club journeyed to Runcorn on Saturday to decide their fixture with the latter club. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors play was confined to twenty minutes each way. During the first half the visitors pressed their op- ponents and scored one try and two minor points to the home team nil. Nothing further was scored on either side until the change of ends. In the second half, which was • played partly in darkness, both teams had a minor point registered to them. At the close of an interesting game the visitors left the field the winners by one try (Dykes) and three minor points to one minor point. For the visitors Barton and Jefferson backs, and Blackledge and Dykes, forwards, played a good game; whilst for the home team all worked hard to secure a victory. Sankey team : Corwell, full back; Barton, Whalley and Woolley, three., quarter backs; Jefferson and Cooper, half-backs; Black. ledge, Dykes Harding, Woods, Jones, Beddle, Brookes, Clarke and Dykes, forwards. WARRINGTON (A) v. ARDWICK (lwr) —The above teams met for the first time this season at Warrington, on Satur- day, before a large assembly, and after a hard fought game Warrington won by one goal and two minors to one minor. The try was obtained by Nevins which Walsh con- verted into a goal. H. Boardman crossed the visitors' line on two occasions, and Bashford once, but the Ardwick cap- tain would not allow the tries, and Warrington rather than kick under pretest gave way. For Ardwick, Greenhalgh and Morris behind, and Broadfoot, Moores, and Hall, for- ward, played well ; whilst Warrington were best repre- sented by H. Boardman and Whittle behind, and Nevins, Forster, Bashford, and Dillon. Teams :—Ardwick: Full back, Drinkwater ; three-quarter backs, S. Wain, Green, H. O'Brien; half backs, A. Morris and G. Gleave ; for- wards, A. Weave, J. Broadfoot (captain), H. Moores, D. Brindley, H. Wark, Wood, Ferriman, Hall, and Hitchings. Warrington : Ashby, full back ; H. Boardman, Belskaw, and Appleton, three-quarter backs ; Walsh and Whittle (captain), half backs ; Lishman, Bashford, Nevins, Molv- neaux, Dillon, ;ones, Mather, Hewitt, and Forster, for- wards.

• WanurnoTore v. Torn:amp/cr.—This match was played at Tottington on Saturday in very inclement weather. Tot- tington bad spared no effort to place a good team in the field ; Warrington, on the other hand, were still without the ; services of Warren and Dillon. The Tottington captain (Fogg) won the toss and elected to play with the wind in his favour. Play eommenced at 3-40, the arrangement be- ing to play two thirty-fives. Frank Turner kicked off, and Fair. Turner rushing up took the ball before it dropped, made a short run, and punted into touch in the home 25. The ball was then thrown out and passed to Barnes, who had a shot at goal. Fogg ran the ball out, and Gilbert getting possession made tracks for the visitors' lines ; being pressed, he passed very unselfishly to Ashton, who secured the first try for Warrington. The place was a very easy one, and Fair. Turner took the kick, but failed to register the major point, to the great disappointment of the War- ringtonians. After the kick out Green was prominent with 'a good run to half-way, then Gilbert passed to Jolley, who carried the game back int, the hems 25. From a scrim- mage Gilbert passed to Barnes, who toek another shot, which, however, was charged down, and the ball was forced into touch. Here Gilbert was rather severely handled and had to retire after playing about ten minutes, and of course, from this to the conclusion of the game Warrington played only 14 men. Frank Turner took Gilbert's place at half back. Coop by a good kick removed the play into tha visitors' 25 for the first time. A scrimmage was formed and the ball heeled out to Hammett, who easily ran in near the touch line. Coop made a splendid kick at goal, the ball just falling short of the bar. Frank Turner kicked out and the Tottington forwards breaking away with a combined dribble forced Massey to save by running into touch in goal. The Warrington forwards following up well, the kick out caused a scrimmage to be formed at centre. Fogg got in a good kick, and Buxton's return was charged down. Directly after Buxton punted to centre, but Fogg again re- turned well, causing Buxton to touch down. Here S. Hough was placed at half back. After the kick out Povey and Hough dribbled to the home 25, but Coop returned to centre, where a scrimmage was formed, and the Tottington forwards coming with a rush forced Buxton again to save. Warrington were again placed en the defensive after the kick out. Then a splendid combined dribble by the visitors' forwards took the ball to the home 25, Walker kicking into teu.;ll. Spencer got possession from the line out and dribbled to half way, then passing to Fogg, who made a determined effort to score, Massey bringing him down in 'grand style almost on the goal line. Then Massey got in a 'good run to centre which brought half time. In the second half Warrington had the best of the play. A scrimmage wee formed at centre, Barnes kicked to the home 25, and once more having the ball passed to him, took his drop, the ball just going outside the bar, Coop touching down. After the kick out Jolley got in a good run and passed to Massey, who kicked. The ball was quickly returned to centre. Massey again doing the needful with a run to the borne 25, and Buxton, who had been changed to half back, dribbled over the line, but In his anxiety to score rolled over the ball, which was kicked dead. Buxton was again prominent after the kick out with a good pass to Barnes, who got his kick into touch. Then Walker made a good run and some smart scrimmaging ended in Massey touching down. The kick out was well followed up, a scrimmage being formed in the visitors' 25. Then Ashton, who had been playing a splendid game throughout, came away with a splendid dribble, only being stopped en the Tottington goal line by Fogg, who touched down Tottington placed another touch down to their credit before call of time, the game ending in a draw, Tottington one try, five minors ; Warrington one try, three minors. The Warrington men were severely handicapped by the absence of their usual half backs, and under the circumstances the result was considered satisfac- tory. The Tottington team has only been beaten once on their own ground for the last seven years, and the usual ill- luck of the Warringtonians undoubtedly deprived them of what would have been a very popular victory. The teams were as follows :—Warrington : Buxton, full back ; T. Barnes, J. Massey, and J. Jolley, three-quarter backs ' • W. Speakman and Gilbert, half backs ; H. Ashton, Fair. Tur- ner, Frank Turner, S. Hough. J. Savage, W. Povey, R. Little. wood, T. Davies, and W. Hayes, forwards. Tottington : Coop, full back; Fogg, Walker, and Dawson, three-quarter backs; Hammett and Barlow, half backs ; Spencer, Hoyle, Green, Leonard, Holt, H. Hammett, Booth, Wilkinson, and Wilson, forwards,

Eanixerowx v. BROMBOROUGH POOL.—Thes'a two teams met at Bromborough Pool on Saturday afternoon to again decide their tie in the first round of the competition for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup. Three weeks ago the Earlestonians were defeated by two goals to one after a miserable exhibition of themselves, but the game was or- dered to be replayed, owing to Bromborough having included in their ranks a player who was ineligible to compete. The second meeting of the teams evoked great interest through• out the district, though it was generally expected the cup,- holders would prove victorious as they were admittedly the beet eleven. The match was played at Broraborough, near New Ferry, and there was a fairly large attendance. The Earlestonians, who were accompanied by a large number of their supporters, were without the services of .T. Duxbury and W. Rich, whose places were respectively filled by W. Lane and H. Holcroft, of the second team. The home team had the best of the wound in the first half, and fairly held their own, Earlestown only being able to score one goal; but on changing ends the visitors soon made it manifest that they intended winning, as they pressed the home team for the greater part of the forty-five minute, the brothers Green and Appleton having little or nothing to do. Ellison was the first to add to the score, the earns player repeated the performance very shortly afterwards,

I while Ogden added a fourth goal after half an hour's play. When the whistle sounded the 'homa team were pointless, while the cupholders had four goals to their credit. For the home team the back division showed splendid defence ; while Ward, Hughes, and Lunt played well forward. Teams i—Earlestown : J. Appleton, goal; J. Green and R. Green, backs; Whalley, Lane, and Bowker, half hacks; J. Ellison, Holcreft, A: Dagnall (captain), J. Sims, and J. Ogden, forwards. Bromborough R. Williams, goal ; T. Adams (captain) and W. Benyon, backs; F. Sidebottom, J. Worthington, and E. 0. Thomas, half backs; T. Jones, T. Simmons, W. Ward, G. Hughes, and J. Lunt, forward.% r- EARLESTOWN WANDERERS T. SOUTHPORT CHRIST CHURCH.—CSIALLENGIS CUP.—This match in the second round of the Liverpool Cep competition was played on the Wanderers' ground on Saturday. The attendance was very good. Champion beat Wainwright in the spin of the coin and took advantage of the wind, and a start was made about, 345. For the first ten minutes the game was even, but the Wanderers then assumed the aggressive and Thom- son notched the first goal. blather (two) and W. Shaw (one) also scored for the Wanderers. At the change of ends the home team led by four goals to none, Champion only handliag the ball once. The second half was also in favour of the Berlestonians, who scored three more goals, whilst Southport again failed, and, the visiting captain with- drawing his men from the field about eight minutes before time OR account of the darkness, and giving the Wanderers the game, the final score read :—Wanderers, seven goals • Christ Church, nil. Teams :—Earlestown Wanderers :T. Champion, goal ; W. Lord and H. Selbie, backs; W. Allison, J. Lowe, and R. Johnson, half-backs; A. Allen and J. Mather, right Wing; T. Thomson, centre; J. Shaw and W. Shaw, left wing. Southport Christ Church G. Hesketh, goal ; H. Moore and W. Moore, backs ; J. Robin- son, J. Evans, and R. Rimmer, half-backs; H. Wainwright and R. Dutton, right wing; F. Rimmer, centre ; R. Black- ledge and U. H. Halsall, left wing. MR. J. E. WARREN. (From The Football Times.) In the subject of our sketch this week, we have a good all-round athlete in Mr. J. E. Warren (or better known, locally speaking, as Ted), captain of the Warrington Foot- hail Club, this being the third time he has held the cap- taincy of that club. Mr. Warren was born at Braunston, in Northamptonshire, on June Bth, 1880. and is, conse- quently, 25 years of age. In height, he is sft. Bin., and is lOst. 10Ibs. in weight, Circumstances removed him, when very young, from the place of his birth, to Dunham Massey district, where he resided on a farm for many years, at- tending school, which was at a distance of six miles, and this daily walk, no doubt, helped to lay the foundation of that muscular ability and stamina which he has since shown on the running track, as well as on the football field. His first attempt at athletics was in the winter of 1876-77, with the Orford Hare and Hounds, which contained in its ranks such men as Andrews, Yeomans, Radcliffe, and Hough. The following spring he won his initial race at Moston, distance one lap of the course, about 730 yard.. His career from this time as an athlete WAS very successful, winning first prizes, among other places, at Widnes, Bir- mingham, Blackley, Swinton, Blackburn, Preston, Chorley, chc., and at this time was considered not far removed from the front rank of northern quarter. milers. As a footballer he commenced his career with the now defunct Padgate Football Club, which, in its day, attained great success, being a much better club than the leading Warrington Football Club, but eventually. this club amalgamated with the Warrington F.C., and Warren was elected captain for the first time ; and as a criterion of his play at this time, be scored more tries ;during the season than all the other players together, at that time, as now, playing in the position of half-back, in- variably playing a grand game. After having held the captaincy of the club twice, he was, practically speaking, on the shelf for some time, until last season when he was induced to den the jersey; and at the end Of a very pros- perous season, his predecessor—Mr. H. Ashton—retiring from the position of captaincy, Mr. Warren was unani- mously elected captain for the third time. Last summer, he was again very successful on the track, winning first prized at different meetings in the flat hurdle faces. His play at half-back is all that could be desired, and he should, undoubtedly, make a name for himself in that po- sition. His fast and powerful runs, and being a splendid tackler, make him a most dangerous opponent. His unself- ish passing reflects great credit upon himself, his passing to his three-quarters being timely and jedicious. Ted is a most popular captain, being genial, affable, and courteotm, and does all in his power to improve, his team, being proud of his men and with just cause, for they are worthy of their captain. In conclusion, we wish him a still more prosperous future, and hope he may lead his men to many victories.

CANDIDATURE OF SIR RICHARD CROSS. MEETING AT PRESCOT. Sir Richard Cross, on Friday night, addressed a meeting of the electors of Eccleston in the Assembly Rooms, Pres- cot, in furtherance of his candidature for the representa- tion of the Newton Division of Lancashire. William Pil- kington, J.P., occupied the chair, and amongst those present were the Revs. 11. A. Macnaghten, J. B. Bolton, and F. Lee, Dr. Gorst, Messrs. S. Tavor, Thomas Swift, W. L. Evans, J. W. Banks, J. Johnson, S. T. Hall, J. Leather. barrow, T. Pilkiogten, W. Newsome, J. Cook, J. Apple- ton, W. Lockwood, A. Waimealey, J. Goldworth, &c.—Sir Ricnard Cross said he c ton before the constituency as the representative of a Government which had done its best and meant to do its best to maintain the honour and dignity of England abroad, to unite the colonies in closer bonds to the mother country, to promote British trade and commerce, and to introduce measures which would not set class against class. but unite them together as one. (Applause.) He held that the Liberal Govern- ment had pursued a line of policy which had tended directly to injure the trade of the comatry. while on the other hand the Conservatives were not ten days in office before they assented to the appointment of a com- mission to go into the whole subject, and be was able to an- nounce that the results of that investigation so far as it had gone would be published to the world in the course of a few days. Speaking on free education Sir Richard expressed the opinion that the honest English working man would spurn the proposal to pay for the education of his children. In every corner of the land the Liberal party had en- deavoured to raise the people against the Church of Eng- land, but the people had refused to be led away, and now, like the cowards and the cravens that they were, the Liberals bad denied that they had started the cry, because they knew that upon that subject they would have been beaten at every hustings. (Applause.)—Mr. S. Taylor moved a resolution declaring Sir Richard Cross to be a fit and proper person to represent the division in the House of Commons, which was seconded by Mr. A. Walmesley.—Mr. T. Swift also supported the resolution, which was carried. MEETING AT CROFT.

On Saturday aiter7n-eeTir-i-gir--iti.C.iTaiei -Cross addressed a meeting of electors in the Board Schools, Croft. Captain Withington occupied the chair, and amongst those present were the Rev. T. P. Kirkman (rector of Croft), Dr. Bide- °Ake, Messrs. Brows-Westhead, J. Pearson. J. Hartley, Arnott Dodson, Cooper, R. Stone, T. Stone, J. Dainteth, W. Stone, Seton, Owen, Comber, Brook, O'Brien, dm. Sir Richard Cross said he had done his best to serve the electors of South-west Lancashire for the last seventeen years, and he asked his constituents whether he had given any pledge which he had not honestly tried to carry out. (Hear, hear.) From the observations which he had made during his progress through the Newton Division he was pretty certain that the right cause was going to win. Alluding to Mr. Gladstone's speeches, he asked the audience whether it was possible from the cloud of words in which be had couched his ideas to make head or tail of what he advised the electors to do. If they read Mr. Gladstone'e speeches throughout they would not find a straightforward, hainest opinion from beginning to end. (Cheers.) In concluding, Sir Richard said he was not seeking their suffrages from any personal motives or ambition of his own, but simply to fight the battle of the great cause which they all had at heart. (Cheers.)—Dr. Bideoake moved a resolution declaring Sir Richard Cross to be a fit and proper person to represent the Newton division.—Mr. J. Dainteth seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Dodson, and carried unanimously.—Sir Richard Cross briefly acknowledged the vote, and moved a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was supported by Mr. Brown-Westhead, supported by the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, and adopted.

_ Mr. W. Grundy, auctioneer, Nottingham, while following the South Notts hounds, on Monday, near Bingham, was thrown from his horse and killed, his neck haying been broken by the fall. MYSTERIOUS ATTEMPTED MURDER.—A mysterious case of supposes' attempted murder and suicide occurred at Derby on Sunday morning. A man and woman were found insensible lying near a haystack by the Derwent. The throats of both were cut, and they were removed to Derby Infirmary, where the wounds were found to be seri- ous. The woman has been identified as the daughter of a Derby publican, named Dreber, and the man's name is Joseph Elliott ; but nothing further is known of him or the circumstances.

DEATH SIANTHNCES.—At Liverpool Assizes, on Monday George Thomas, a coloured seaman, 29, was convicted of the murder of Margaret Askin, by shooting her whilst they were drinking together in a public-house in Beaufort-street, Toxteth Park, on September 9th. Jealousy of another coloured seaman, named Powell, was the motive for the crime' and, before sentence of death was passed open him, the prisoner expressed his regret that he bad not shot Powell as well as the woman,—Jos. Flynn, 17, boiler scaler, charged with the murder of Edwin Pearson, a carter, by stabbing him in Balliol-road, Bootle, en September 19th, was found guilty, with A strong recommendation to mercy on account of his youth. Sentence of death was passed.

DEFEAT OF THE SERVIANS NEAR SLIVNITZA.. 3,000 KILLED AND WOUNDED. SOFIA, WEDNEsDAY.—An important engagement has been fought at Slivnitza. The Bulgarian troops, under the com- mand of Prince Alexander, attacked and carried by assault the Servian positions at Gornimalo and Dolnimalo, by which the safety of Slivnitza was threatened: Another such vic- tory will force the Servians to retire from the Dragoman Pass. Prince Alexander himself displayed the greatest bravery throughout the engagement: (From the Daily IVeicB.) , SOFIA, WEDNESDAY.--The Bulgarian division from Trn and Bresnitza has outflanked the Servian position at Dragoman. Prince Alexander displayed much gallantry, and was in the thick of the fight. He led the attack from Sliv- *Rea. The Servians were completely routed, and retreated in disorder, endeavouring to reach their own country. Many prisoners were taken, amongst them being 200 cavalry soldiers. Nightfall put an end to the pursuit. It was, however, to be continued at the dawn. SOFIA. WEDNESDAY, LATER.—The Servians, having ral- lied during the night, made a stand again on the road to Tzaribrod, but were soon outflanked, defeated, and again put to flight. Had the Bulgarians possessed sufficient cavalry, the enemy would have been annihilated. The Servians lost ten field-pieces and 356 horses. It is estimated that they left 3.000 killed slid wounded on the field. Many prisoners were made. I saw to-day twenty of them, all weak, wretched-looking men. GREEK APPEAL TO FRANCE. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—M. de lireycinet this morning received, but only in his private capacity, M Philemon, President of the Municipal Council at Athens, who ap- pealed for French sympathy, reminding the Minister of the traditional goodwill entertained by France for Greece. The Minister replied that he was unable to enter into explana. Hone on this subject with M. Philemon. REPORTED CAPTURE OF WIDDIN. BELGRADE, WEDNESDAY EVENING.—Queen Natalie re- ceived a telegram at six o'clock this evening from Zaitchar, announcing the fall of Widdin. Part of the Morava division, under Colonel Topalovitch, has taken Radomir 'after severe fighting. Four hundred prisoners have just arrived here by railway from the front. The Prefect of Belgrade announces that all the Servian Inhabitants of Trn who have taken refuge in Servia are now at liberty to remain. SOFIA, WEDNESDAY EVENING —Another important en- gagement took place at Slivnitza to-day. In the battle near that place yesterday 25,000 Servians, with seven batteries of artillery, were engaged, while the Bulgarians disposed of only 15,000 men, not including artillery. The wounded are being conveyed here from the front. Troops are arriv- ing here from Eastern Roumelia. THE BURMESE WAR. BRITISH PROCLAMATION.—CAPTURE OF A BUR- MESE WAR VESSEL RANGOON, SATURDAY.—A British proclamation to the BUT mese people assures them that none will be molested in the enjoyment of their privileges, in their commercial pur- suits, or in the exercise of their religious duties. Buddhism will rem.in the religion of the country. All native civil and military (Acme will be retained provisionally on con- dition that they continue faithfully to discharge their duties. At the same time all are warned that the killing or maltreatment of any British soldiers will .entail a heavy fine. The district officers are instructed to look no longer to the Illootdaw or the Mengyees at-Mandalay for orders, and they are assured that no harm will befall them through compliance with these instructions. Theebaw, concludes the proclamation, will never rule the country again THEYETAITO, SATURDAY. -- One of King Theebaw's steamers on the Irrawaddy, carrying a large quantity of ammunition and manned by 200 men, has been captured by the launch Kathleen, armed with two howitzers and commanded by Lieut. French, of the Turquoise. The Burmese crew were driven overboard by the artillery fire of the launch Kathleen, and of the Government steamer accom- panying her. The British boarded the Burmese vessel after the engagement, and proceeded up the river. Three thousand of the Burmese are reported to be at Fort Kuligon, which is said to be stockaded. The British station at Ma.utkin has h?en attacked by the Burmese, who were repulsed, but not before they had looted the village.—

Times. THEYETMYO, SATURDAY.—The armed steamer Resistance I and a launch in reconnoitring to•day found a stockaded ,position with guns twelve miles across the frontier. They engaged these and captured a Burmese steamer carrying am- munition. The Burmans raided a frontier villiage to-day.— Daily News. THEIRTMYO (FROM STEAMER TRANBYDINES), SUNDAY. --The Burmese retired to-day from some small forts on the frontier. A determined resistance is probable at Minhla. Mr. E. Andreino and other Europeans are detained at Man- dalay, where all was quiet on the 11th, but a Palace revo- lution is expected. CAPTURE OF THE BURMESE POSITION AT MINHLA. THREE HOURS' FIUHTING. RANGOON, WEDNESDAY. The Burmese position at Minhla was carried by assault at ODO o'clock yesterday , afternoon after a fight which lasted for three hours. The 'British casualties were hut slight—one officer was killed and three wounded. By this victory the way to Mandalay

is cleated. Prior to the capture of Minhla Major General Norman advanced six miles up the left bank of the Irrawaddy, and occupied Sengboung-Weh after firing two shells. Major General Prendergast, operating on the right bank, shelled the Kuligon Fort, which was attacked in the rear and taken. The guns defending it were spiked. (Fuom THE "DAILY NEWS.") THEYETHYO, WEDNESDAY, 7-30 AM.—On the river below Minbla the Burmese abandoned the forte opposite Seng- boung-Weh te-day without fighting. We landed a party, who spiked the guns on the west bank, and also burned a stockade in a village on the east bank. The Welsh Fusiliers met with no resistance. M. corvette Opal to co-operate with the expe- dition organised to ascertain the fate of the members of the Sydney Geographical Society's expedition. THE CAROLINE ISLANDS. ,ROME, WEDNESDAY.—The German Government having acquiosced in the Pope's decision in regard to the Caroline Islands question the matter is regarded as settled. It now only remains to give a definite form to the recommendation made by his Holiness. THE VICEROY OF INDIA'S CAMP. JODHPORE, WEDNESDAY.—The Viceroy and suite arrived here on Sunday last, and were received near the town by that Maharajah. The Viceregal party immediately drove to the camp, which was luxuriou-ly fitted up. The road along the route was lined by a brilliant gathering of 10,000 people, including the flower of the Marwar nobility and their followers. Lord Dufferin was impressed by the splendour of the gathering, and remarked that ha had never witnessed a more striking scene. FRANCE.—MINISTERIAL DECLARATION. PARIS, MONDAY.—M. Brisssn, the French Premier, read an important statement of his policy in the Chamber to-day. He pointed out the necessity of reorganising the national finances, and said that the Government would not hesitate, if necessary, to impose fresh taxation. The statement "repelled "the idea of abandonment with regard to Tonquin, and explained that fresh credits would be demanded for the operations in Madagascar. SOUTH AFRICA.—THREATENED HOSTILITIS. DURBAN, MONDAY.—Hoetilities threaten to break out be- tween the Transvaal Government and Massouw and other natives on the south-west border of the Rapublia, with whom General Joubert has failed to come to an amicable settle- ment. M. van Niekirk, the Commissioner, has fled for his life.

MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND- SPEECH AT WEST CALDER. On Tuesday, at various points along the route from Dalmeny to West Calder, Mr. Gladstone was again the subject of popular demonstrations. These, which commenced at Dalmeny, were continued at Craigleith, where a special train awaited him, and they reached their highest pitch of enthusiasm where apparently all the population, excepting those who had already been fortunate enough to secure places at the meeting, were assembled either at the railway statical or in the main street of the village to welcome the veteran statesman. The special train left the Craigleith station of the Caledonian Railway at half-past one o'clock, and arrived at West Calder at a quarter to three, where Mr. Gladstone was received with hearty and pro- longed cheering. In his drive through the village, Mr. Gladstone found that his constituents there, not content with this reception, had decorated almost every house in honour of the occasion. Two or three triumphal arches were erected, one of them bearing the motto, " Right welcome back, Friend of the People." The others also bore appropriate inscriptions, and expressions of welcome or attach- ment were likewise displayed from many private dwellings, with the addition of such floral festoons and flags as their decorative resources would per- mit. In the place of meeting itself similar festive adornments were conspicuous, especially above and around the platform, where the words "Our fran- chise hopes now realised" were prominent in red letters. The first outburst of cheering within the hall was when the Countess of Rosebery entered it. Punctually at three o'clock Mr. Gladstone himself arrived, and was greeted with enthusiastic and pro- longed cheering. The right hon. gentleman was accompanied by Mrs. Gladsttne, Miss Gladstone, and Mr. Henry Gladstone. There were also present on the platform Professor Bryce, M.P., Mr. P. Mo- Lagan, M.P., Major Hamilton, M.P., Mr. J. Cowan, of Beeslach, chairman. Mr. Gladstone was on his feet at thirteen minutes past three o'clock ready for work, and looking the picture of health. The moment be opened his lips, too, it was found that his voice was stronger and more tuneful than on Wed- nesday Week, and, satisfied with themselves and their mem- ber, the West Calder electors settled down to listen. Cleverly assorting a former speeeh at West Calder with the address presented to him, Mr. Gladstone reminded the electors of his promise in IRO to promote franchise reform, and accepted their testimony that the pledge had been re- deemed. With equal skill and adroitness he narrated hie latest victory, by which he had secured twelve . additional seats for Scotland, and had thus in spite of the opposition of the Tory peers, and the temporising policy redressed to some extent the electoral inequality from which Scotlapd had hitherto suffered. He re-stated and re-emphasised political union among Liberals al the chtef object of his present *visit, and playfully disposed of Mr. Parnell'e isvita- tation conveyed to him through the confidential channel of the public Press that he should frame a. plan for the settle- ment of the Irish question, and thus play a part of the volun- teer physician for the people of Ireland before they had made a choice of their authorised doctors, at the same time sug- gesting that a Tory Government who owed so much to Irish members ought first to have been offered it, and satirically commenting on the silence of tbe Tory leaders on this sub- ject. Referring to the subject of diseetablishment, he made it clear that he had . Scotland as well as England in his mind when last week he made what be described as his conscientious declarations. He encountered a repetition of the demonstration made in the Free Assembly Hall, last week, when be included the disestabllehment of the Scottish Church in the list of re- forms which be could not for the sake of popularity promise to undertake. Loud cries of "Yes " and "No" contending for the mastery interrupt-d the orator, but by and by tha strife was allayed by Mr. Gladstone's prompt ex- planation that he was not speaking of the merits of the question, but only of the policy of including it in the pro- gramme of the coming •Parliament. Els further sought to pacify and console the disestablishment party by pointing out.the necessity for an acceleration Of the legislation pro- cedure of the House as the means of removing the arrears which had accumulated through the obstruction of otter questions, and by recognising its loyal nonconformant Liberals as the backbone of the party. He explained fur- ther that he accepted its severance from the Scotch and from the English branch of the Church and State question. But at the same time he maintained that this severance could not presently be effected, nor din he give the slightest hint how it ever could be. I It cannot be said that the acquiescence of the audiesice in that political prescription was by any means cordial : on the contrary, the meeting was most irresponsive in temper and attitude, which became all the more marked by the energy and heartiness with which the audience shortly afterwards enforced Mr. Gladetone's condemnation of the tactics of the mischievous Fourth Party and the obstruc- tionists, or the rigging cheer which hailed his declaration that there was no error committed by his Government in connection with the Soudan that was not fostered by the Tory opposition. He acknowledged, however, that the Government had settled the Afghan frontier controversy on the basis of the lines laid down by their predecessors, and cheerfully accorded to them the credit of having on the subject agreed with the Liberals. He thankfully acknow- ledged, too, that so far as he knew the facts, Lord Salisbury seemed to be following a wise and practical policy in the Eastern crisis, caused by tbe union of the two Balgarias, and aggravated by the war just begun with Servia, a war which he described as one of the most melancholy spec- tacles that bad ever met his eyes. As the critic of the Ministers, however, he severely censured Lori R. Churchill and Sir M. Hicks-Beach for the countenance they gave to the attack of the adminstration of justice in Ireland during Lord Spencer's viceroyalty, and unsparingly ridiculed and denounced the Royal Commission on trade as a pieee of quackery. Mr. Gladstone concluded by an eloquent recital of the beneficial measures of legisla• tion passed by the Liberals, and by an earnest appeal for continued confidence in the party for what they had done in the past. The right bon. gentleman spoke throughout with remarkable vigour. and the closing passages were delivered vith telling effect.

_ --- Mr. Gladstone spent a quiet day of retirement at Lord Rosebery's seat, Dalmeny House, on Wednesday. During the forenoon he was engaged, as usual, with his correspond- ence, but in the afternoon he went out, notwithstanding the severe wintry weather now prevailing, and took a walk in Dalmenv Park. It teas now been definitely arranged that the ceremony of unveiling the old City Cross shall take place on Monday hf ternooo, when Mr. Gladstone will be entertained to cake and wine in the Council Chamber, and will deliver an address. Preparations are being actively made for the Dalkeith meeting on Saturday, Mr. Gladstone spent Thursday quietly at Dalmeny. A.B the weather in the morning was fine and bracing, he walked out in the grounds with Lord Rosebery, and in the after- noon remained indoors attending to correspondence.

The Convocations of Canterbury and York were dissol- ved on Wednesday, and an order in Council was issued directing new writs to be issued for electing new mem- bers, the writs to be returnable on the 13th of January. THE LATE EARL OF SHATTBSRIIRY.-10 order to perpet- uate the memory of the late Earl of Shaftesbury, a scholar- ship has been established in connection with the Exeter Hall (London) University Classes. It is of the annual value of 12 guineas, secured by open competition, and is intended to encourage and assist young men (under 21) to graduate at the London University. r Tim Alaimo:nen CASE:A liberal response has been made to Mr. Poland's appeal on behalf of the Armstrongs. Several offers have been made of a home for Eliza Armstrong, but Mr. Poland is of opinion that she should receive some more education, and should then be trained for domestic service. If there are sufficient funds, a small sum will be re- served for her, to provide a small owry in case of her marriage. ArramrrED Mt:mum—Thomas Smith, who attempted to murder his mother-in-law and sister-in-law on the 19th October, at Hetton-le-hole, in the county of Durham, by cutting their throats, was on Wednesday committed for trial. The evidence allowed that the prisomer's attack was very desperate and determined. The mother-in-law was in so precarious a condition that she had to be as- sisted from the box by two friends. The prisoner fainted in tke dock whilst the evidence was proceeding. PARLIAMENT is dissolved; there is no SUCH being at the moment we write as an but the time is rapidly approaching when the, electors—including the Two MiwoNs--wil be called upon to choose their representi tives for a new House of Commons. Both political parties have been engaged for the past few weeks in laying their views before the various constituencies; and the lines are now so sharply defined that he who rorls may read. The Tories have, as usual, bee° hard up for a policy; and we would put it any elector who has been looking on dis- passionately whether hp can lay his hand on a single thing and say—" This is what we shall get from the Tories if they are retune°, to St. Stephens; but we shall get nothing 0,4, the kind from the Liberals." The answer, n the truth be spoken, must be an emphatiC " No." The Liberals, on the other hand, have a programme well defined, and univer" sally accepted by the party. There hava.„6 been some differences of opinion as a'" pw rhoegt rhaen ir ma ed d; i tbi ou nt st es rheo ub lady e b be e me na dn me ateo tn; as tO' the importance of the proposals which cool within its scope. It is recognised, now tilt( Mr. GLADSTONE has finally spoken, that the tasks which he has assigned the Liberait, party will, in case of its return to office, fal tax its powers; indeed, we cannot but thin , that the inhabitants of the United Kingdol3! may regard themselves as fortunate if the 4 • are all accomplished within the next years. To take the first—Reform of Froi. cedure—it is imperatively necessary that something should be done to ensure that tb Parliamentary machine shall do its work and t run smoothly. At present, as an instrunt° for the transaction of the nation's businesSi it is like an old stage coach in an age railways. The Liberals see this, and are !ready with a remedy. The Tories ei,rll,le; I don't or won't see that a change is neeoelf getting business done is not in their way ; they can be said to have a policy at all, a policy of "masterly inactivity.' On the Land Question the Tories will nothing worthy of the name of reform, cause their fate as a party is bound up W*3 that of the landed aristocracy. They make lb their business to defend rather than abolis t class privileges. The Liberals will strike ad the root in abolishing the laws of entail primogeniture; .the Tories propose to I°Pd off a branch here and there, leaving the deta tree to cumber the ground.
