*r,'`lrYism of twenty years ago, when those who pleaded for a voice in ,the making of the laws they were called won to obey were derided as "the swinish multitude" and ",the great unwashed." If. the working-men of St. 'Helens will vote for Mr. SETON-KARR. after being spoken of in the mass as rogues and atieves, they deserire that trampling Ilnder foot which he would seem disposed to accord ,them. Then this question of local Sceif-gov.ernment involves Home Rule, in one 'Prrn or another, for Ireland ; and this the '"iberals are prepared to grant. Mr. GLAD- STONE has pledged himself on the subject, and none know better than Irishmen that the tel‘x P R m r R ,has always kept his word with ,""n--that be is the greatest benefactor to Ireland that the Sitter Isle has ,ever known. 'will they turn to Lord SALISBURY in the hope `4sf better things-Lord SALISBURY who a few Yde/Irs ago was never so happy as when he was denouncing the Liberal Government for not ar_asPing Irishmen with an iron hand; Lord Zu-Esituay who has bitterly opposed every -",,enture that had for its object the bettering , tive condition of the Irish people Lord ePzi's•ginty who brought reland to the verge a revolution by rejecting the Irish Corn- rtensation Bill ? The idea is preposterous; c repugnant to reason; it is a mocker 7 of onninion-sense. Workingmez, whether Irish arr nglish, who look to Toryism for benefits r he Strangely deluded; they may as well ea- e ct “gs from thorns, or grapes from a: l. 0 galble bush. Toryism, as Mr. DISRAELI' riee Said, is the mule of polities, that en- genders nothing.

inn!="2222 ; ,WEDNESDAY next is big with fate for the oabitants of St. Helens. They will then " called upon, for the first time, to choose representative for the borongh which owes much to Free Trade Liberalism. What 1 111 the new electors do ? Will they turn 'oeir backs upon themselves by recording a !Tie for the party that has for generation `ter generation gtrugrcled to prevent political -)"fer passing into the hands of the people; ; r will they, like men who possess sense and are„ not without gratitude, vote for the party that has at last succeeded in bringing 'every householder within the pale of the, constitution ? We cannot think that work- ,nle will be false to themselves; and if "Le 7 vfo are true, and firm to the truth, they will orte tn - a man for Colonel GAMBLE, who has generation been a champion of the peO- P.'e s cause. He helped in days gone by to Five the toiler untaiced bread; and, if returned 1?, St. Stephens, he will resist the insidious' prept which is again being made to nut a cai dii the arm', 9f Jife, He helped to , Istablish Free Trade, which has made tngland as a trade centre the envy of the civilised world ; and he will stoutly oppose the designs a intriguing capitalists who preach un-Fair Trade with a View to getting rich by taxing the whole community. He lent a willing hand to those who have been striving for so long to obtain the franchise; and he is desirous that throughout the kingdom—in Ireland as well as England the voters shall be masters (5f their own affairs. Mr. SETON-KARR, the Tory candidate, has nothing to re- °,lllltend him -- except that he is some- "pure son-in-13:w. The nation is getting tired 1 0 el • the w of this kind; and requires men in -n,"e new Parliament of proved fitness for the fait work that is yet to be done. Let the rectors of St. Helens remember that the vote • a'Sk but the means to an end—a reform of irlseS which will put all classes on an equal °tiog and tell the Tories at the ballot box they have not a single claim upon the People of st. Helens.

Tuesday 15,a bad day alike for master and man; it is 4.characteristic result of Tory management and ' .4 gry intrigue. THE Election Address, Of Mr. J. T. BRUNNER will be found in 'another column. It is a lengthy document; but no one who reads it will think it one word too long, for that may be said of it which used to be said of COBDEN'S speeches—it is alive at every point. The Liberal candidate for the North- • wich Division is no half-and-halt man; he is whole-souled ; he does not sit on the fence— he puts his hand to the plough. We can well believe that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN would like to see Mr. BRUNNER in Parliament ; he is a candidate after Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S own heart. Let those who may falter ig their faith —if there be any— peruse Mr. BRUNNER' 6 Address, and we venture to say they will be strengthened and re- freshed. He accepts the four central features of •Mr. GLADTONE'S programme.; i but he knows what this involves, and he sets forth his views in vigorous' and telling language. The Liberals or tilt; ,Northwich Division have a candidate of whom any' con- stituency might be proud, and they ought to make every exertion—every sacrifice---to ensure his triumphant return to Parliament.

Mn. BRUNNER'S CANDIDATURE.—Next Saturday a mass meeting of the working-men supporters of Mr. &Mina will be held in the Theatre, Runcorn. The meeting is to 'be presided 'pier by Mr. J. Handley, and addresses will be given by Mr. Brunner, Mr. C. M. Percy, the miners' candidate for Ince Division, T. Snape, and several other gentlemen. As there is sure to be a crowded gathering, those who want to secure seats will do well to be early in attendance. THE "WiDrass EXAMINER " Office has been removed to Victoria-road. Mr. E. Martley, chief agent for the Examiner, is authorised to receive advertisements and news paragraphs All printing orders sent to him will receive prompt atten- tiod. THE IRISH VOTE rig RuNconN —The Irish Nationalists of Runcorn have decided to vote as Mr. Parnell dictates. ZION FREE CHIIREII, WIDNES.—The anniversary sermons were preached in the United Methodist Free Church. Oak- land-street, on Sunday, by the Rev. D. Brook, B. A., of Liverpool. There were goad congregations at each service. On Mondaylevening a lecture on "Haunted Rouses" was delivered to a large audience by the Rev. Silas Hooking, of Southport. Mr. S. Pslin presided. FRYER STREET RAGGEDScaom, RIINCORN.—A school intended for the reception of p3or and uncared-for children has been commenced in Fryer-street. One evening during the week will be devoted to educational work, and another to temperance effort. The Committee are making earnest application for cast-off clothes, and any donations of this sort will be properly distributed amongst the children. CONCERT AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday evening a con- cert in aid of St. Ambrose Courch funds was held in the Mission-room, Page-lane. There was a numerous gather- ing. The ladies and gentlemen who assisted in the pro- ceedings were—Misses Gardner, Finney, Scrymgeour, Gorse, Prescott ; Messrs. George Barton, George Barton, jun., Rowed, J. Taylor, and Merrill. Mr. 0. M. Barton acted as accompanist in an excellent manner. Mr. George Barton, the eminent Lancashire tenor, was in very good voice, and his singing was greatly enjoyed. His son is also the possessor of A fine voice, and bids fair to emulate his father. The different songs, solos, and choruses were ren- dered in a most effective manner. By the kindness of Mr. John Valentyne, of Halton View, the singers gave their services gratuitously. BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY, RUNCORN BRANCH. —The annual meeting of the Runcorn Auxiliary of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the small hall of the Public hall on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance. Mr. W. J. Shore presided, and he was supported by the Revs W. Dickens Lewis, of Shrewsbury (deputation). G. Wood, J. D. Thomas, E. Williams, W. Preston, Secretary, and Mr. J. Humphreys.—The Chairman, after a graceful reference to the late president of the I Society, Lord sheftesbury. spoke of the unsectarian char. acter of the Society, and the valuable work it had accom- plished at home and abroad during the 81 years of its existence.—Mr. Humphreys read the report of the Auxiliary which showed that the subscriptions amounted to upwards of £4O. a decrease of £2 10s. 4d. en the previous year. The Rev. W. Preston delivered an addrese, in which he said the Bible Society stood far above other societies, because With- out its aid Missionary societies could not prosecute their labours in evangelising and bringing those people who stood in need of Christian light to a knowledge of the truth. The deputation also delivered an address upon' the work of the I Society, and the customary vote of thanks concluded the proceedings. COAGULINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. Is. 2s : postage 2nd. PROTECTION.—The Preston Guardian for Wednes- day says sketches on Monday we came across an extrect 'of In glancing at some old historical exceptional interest just now. It referred to what took place two centuries ago precisely this year Time, James 11., 1685 Report from the Com- mittee of the House of Commons on the woollen trade. Resolved,—That it is the opinion of this committee that the East India Company woollen manufacturer. That calicoes, &C., import- ing raw and unwrought silk is prejudicial to the by brought from the East Indies are prejudicial to the woollen manufacturer. That East India wrought silks are likewise prejudicial to the woollen manufacturer. That a clause be inserted in the Bill for Woollen Manufacture to enforce women, under the degree of gentlewomen, to wear hats made of wool, as for-' merly I A committee of the House was appointed to consider ways and means to keep up th, price of wool and corn.' How amazing that the lapse of two great and progressive centuries should witness such a terrible retrogression as that clearly apparent in the attempt to make bread and the various necessaries of life scarcer and dearer for. the masses of working folks in order to secure the landowner his high rents! Had not the Committee of 1685 and the Commission of 1885 practically the same object? Was ever the political intelligence of a Free People treated with more sovereign contempt?" , • • Public Analysts have submitted rADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and therein:tit has always proved its great value as a sue taining and nourishing beverage. (Hear, hear.) In many parts of the country farmers held their land at the will of the landlord. 'lbis was a moat extra- ordinary tenure, and one that, except tindervery exceptional circumstances, could hardly I.e possible. It was true that in this neighbourhood, and also in other parts of England, they had good landlords, 'who had not disturbed their tenants, and who had not raised a rack rent upon the tenants, but they must remember that they had not to legislate only for good landlords; they had to legislate for bad landlords. What was the position of a bed landlord. It was possible that the tenant might spend a great deal of labour upon the farm, and he might be forced to quit by the landlord raising his rent upon the improvements which the tenant bad made, or, as formerly, before they had the protection of the ballot, if he voted against the landlord. How was this to be remedied? It seemed to him very simple and clear that the tenant when he quits his farm should have full compensation for any improvement he had made, and that the landlord ought not to be permitted to raise the rent upon the improvements. (Applause and interruption.) How was it that the tenant farmers of Eng- land should for the last 50 years have had the franchise and not been able to insist upon the legislation protecting their improvements? It was because they had been bamboozled by the Tories. (Cheers and hisses.) The landlords and Tories told the farmers that if the Corn LAWS were abolished they would be ruined, and that therefore the Liberal Ree formers were not the friends of the tenant farmers. In 1841, mainly through the votes of the tenant farmers, the Tories were returned to power. Would they believe it, that before that Parliament was ended the Tory Ministry abolished the Corn LAWS altogether' (Cheers, and a voice "Shame.") Evidently that gentleman thought the Corn Laws should not have been aholished. He was not of that opinion. (Applause.) In 1852 there was great depression in agriculture. LECTURE ON DISESTABLISHMENT.

- - - Under the auspices of the Church Defence Society, a lec- ture en Disestablishtnent was given in Waterloo-road School, Widnes, on Mond ty evening, by the Rev. J. W. Rhodes, vicar of St. Chad's, Everton. The Rev. J.Wright Williams, vicar, presided, and in opening the proceedings said that meeting was not in any degree a political meeting. The clergy had the right, and he hoped they would exercise that right, to consider which parties in the State were the best io their opinion. But there were times and seasons when Church questions came into view, and he hoped the time was approaching when each Churchman would be a Churchman first, and a party man aft( rwards. (Applause.) They were told that the Church was not before the coun- try, but he quoted from the report of the Liberation Society to show that out of 581 candidates, 462 were mole or less pledged to disestablishment. He did not tell them how to vote ; it was uot his duty to do that, but it was their duty to do the best.. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. W. Rhodes then delivered his lecture, in which he declared tilt it was abso- lutely untrue that the State ever looked abtot for a reliion to establish. It was absolutely true that the Church estab- lished the State. It was absolutely untrue that the State had esclowed the Church. But it was absolutely true that the Church had endowed the State. He denied that the clergy were in any menee State paid, and stated the State no more gave them tithes than she gave people food. If the Church were disendowed the people who would suffer most would be the poor laity.—The customary vote of thanks were passel.

MR, BRITNNG'R'S CANDMATURE. LIBERAL MEETING AT WESTON. Last night a meeting of the friends and suppor ters of Mr. Brunner, the ,Liberal candidate, took place in the large room ,of the Prospect Inn, Wes- ton. Amongst those present were the Candidate, the Bev. J. D. Thomas,. Mr. and Mrs Joynson (of the Brine Scheme, Runcorn), Messrs. James Hand- ley, J.P., J. R. Frith, T. Jepson, G. E. King (North- wichi, J. Gayter, S. Dutton, Whitehead, William Hulse, and T. Whitby, Mr. T. lI&NDLEY presided, and in a brief speech said on Tuesday week they would be called upon to say whether they would suppor(that party which for the last fifty years had passed so many excellent measures of reform for the good of all the people in the. country, or whether they would support the party which had opposed all those re- forms. (Applautie.) Mr. BRUNNER, who v as enthusiastically received, dealt with the question of trade. He celled Oat Free Trade when every man was left to buy what he liked, where he liked, and sscheap as he could get it. (Hear, hear.) What was called Fair Trade was just this—that a lot of fussy fools; And not a few knaves were to o to London to a Government office and settle what the people were to pay for things, and where they were to buy them. (Laugh- ter.) There was no doubt depression in trade, but just those countries were worst off that had this bad system of "Fair Trade." The number of men out of employ in the United States, where they had this system, was simply appalling. Wherever they went, from north to south, in America there were these men out of employ to such an extent that the streets were almost crowded with them. He ridiculed the idea of adopting a protective tariff. In showing what the Liberal party had lone for tke alkali trade, be mentioned the abolition of the excise duties upon glass and soap, and the result had been, an enormous lift to the alkali trade. (Applaase.) He described in forcible terms the iniquities of the death duties, the law of entail and primogeniture, and the unjust condi- tions under which the farmer struggled. He wanted to abolish these bad laws, and replace them by good laws. (Cheers) Mr. WiliTenna,. moved a test:4olga et confidence and support in Mr. Brunner in a 'suitable speech. Mr. S. Durrow seconded the motion in a few remarks that were loudly applauded. Mr. KING, of Northwich, delivered a speech in support, narrating the achievements of the Liberal party in the past. , The motion was carried enthusiastically.

LONDON, THURSDAY. To-day dawned amid a concatenation of circum- stances rare in its occurrence. We have a little war of our own on hand in Burmah. The South- East of Europe is in the throes of battle; and we have no Parliament. There is the House of Lords, it is true, which, unlike the Old Guard, never dies, but sometimes surrenders. The House of Lords is intact as far as its membership is concerned, al- though, as the Gazette has dissolved Parliament it could not very well meet at Westminster, and cer- tainly has no legislative power. But if a bewildered nation anxious to go to the highest fount of human wisdom and statesmanship urgently desired the counsel of the Peers there would be nothing against their meeting in Exeter Hall or Sangers Theatre or some other public building, and taking counsel to- gether. They are not likely to be called upon thus to sacrifice tlieir time; but it is well to know, now that we have not got in the land a man qualified to write M.P. after his name, that there is still all the material for making a House of Lords. As to the war in Burmah, it has proceeded with a swiftness and regularity that betokens admirable preparation. On Tuesday the Burmese position at Minhla was carried by assault, the Burmese ap- parently making a desperate stand. There was three hours fighting, an officer and three men killed with twenty-eight men and officers woun- ded. Minhla is a fort lying about thirty miles within the Burmese frontier, and holds the gate to Mandalay. There is now nothing to bar the way to the capital, and before you go to press you may have received news that the British flotilla is moored off Mandalay and that the Lord of the Sun and Moon, the maniacal monarch, who, if he had lived in England, would long ago have been locked up for being drunk and disorderly, has fled. Pos- sibly a worse fate may await him, for Mandalay has a long score to settle with its drunken tyrant, and may seize this favourable opportunity. In the south-east of Europe the war is of a much more determined and bloodthirsty character than that in which Burmah almost passively figures. War was declared between Bulgaria and Servia "at six o'clock last Saturday morning "--it is as well to be precise in these matters. Servia has attempted to excuse its agression by affirming that Bulgaria began it. But there is a general consensus of opinion that Servia has behaved in a determinedly bullying spirit, and has forced the war on Bulgaria. This determination to fight with or without excuse is a serious matter, because it seems to indicate that there is some one behind urging Servia on. This can be none other than Austria, and there are rumours, likely at any moment to become asser- tions, that Russia will appear on the other side at i the back of Bulgaria. It s only Prince Alexander that the Czar is wrath with, and that because an outbreak for which Russia has long been preparing was too precipitably brought about by the Prince. There is one satisfactory feature in the war, since war there must be, that it is likely to be short and. sharp: The forces of Servia far out-number those of Bulgaria. The Servians, it is true, have met with a reverse at Slivnitza. But that will soon be repaired, and then there will be little to stand between the invaders and Sofia.

MR. GEO. WooDS AND THE EDITOR OF "THE EXAMINER."

The following letters --reference to which was made in our last issue—have been sent to Mr. George Woods, in consequence of a gross accusation which he made at a public meeting : Ezaminer uific.. Warrington. ber 11th, 1885. To Gore Woods, E-q. Sir,—One of our reporters who was present at the Tory , meeting, in North-West Ward on Monday evening, states that at that meeting you made use of the following language in reference to myself, as editor of the Examiner :—"1 ask which do you consider the greatest weatbarcock, the man who gives sound reasons for turning round, or the man who, at a moment's notice, leayas the editorial charge of a rank Conservative paper, and in a neek accepts the position of elitor of a Radical paper without giving any reason why he no changes." I assume that you would not even by linplieatior, make such a charge against a journatist without haying, or be- lieving you had, adequate evidence of its accuracy. I. shall be obliged, therefore, if you will immediately furnish me with your evidence and authority for the charge, or at once withdraw it.
I give the charge an unqualified contradiction, and I need hardly say that I purpose publishing the correspondence on the subject. —Your truly,
JOHN WALKER.
Examiner Office, Warring! on, November 13th, 1885 To George Woods, Eq.. . .

beg to remind you that you hays not yet replied to my letter of the 11th inst. I hope you are not under the necessity of hunting for evidence in support of an aCelMi• Von after you have made it —Yours truly, JOHN WALKER.

Mr. Woods has not replied; but he made a refer- ence to the matter at a meeting last evening, trying to "shuffle out" without attempting in the slightest degree to sustain his ac- cusation. As he cannot answer the conun- drum he has put, and has shown himself devoid of common courtesy, we append, by way of solution, the following letters we have received from other quarters. He has himself to blame, if he should find ths,t neither slander nor cowardice are safe harbours of refuge t•—• (Pram James Beaty, Esq. JP., leader of the Liberal party in Blackburn.) Reform Club, Victoria-street, Blackburn, November 12th, 1885. Dear Mr. Walker,—l see that one of the Tories hag bten speaking, of you as a political weathercock, who had occupied an editorial chair alternately of both a Liberal and Tory newspaper. If the man had known you as well and as long as I have, he would not have made such a charge, unless with a reckless disregard of truth. Having been familiar witn your manner of life for more than twenty years, I an certain that you could not be induced to write against your convictions for any salary that a Tory newspaper proprietor would offer, nor have you ever done so.—Very truly yours,
JAMES BEADS.

• (Front Johit Hawking s, Esq., manager ,of "The (Antral Press.") The Central Press, 22, Parliamentstreet. tendon, S.W., November 12th, 1885. Dear Mr. Walker,—ln reply to your inquiry, it is a matter of regret to me, that at the time you were connected with the Editorial Depirtment of the Central Press, it was known that, that, instead of being a good Conservative, you were pronounced and an irreclaimable Liberal. I am bound to add, however, that the duties which de- volved upon you, and which you discharged with marked ability, were altogether of'a non-political character, and could be honestly performed by a Radical, or even a Repub- lican politician, without in the least compromising his poltical integrity. Trusting that you may grow wiser as you grow older, and be converted from the error of your Liberal ways, to the true faith of Conseryalism,—Believe me, yours faithfully, JNO. /UW1E114703, Manager.
John Walker, Esq.. Examiner Office, Warrington.

(Front W. E. Briggs, Esq., if.!'. for Blackburn.) Moss Field, Fleasington, Blackburn, 12, 11, 1885. Dear Walker,—What idiat has been aspersing the purity co your pothical faith and consistency? You are, and have al,%ays bsen, a thnromibly earnest Liberal. Treat him with contempt—Yours sincerely,
' W. E. BRIMIS
There is nothing to add, except to suggest that Mr. Woods would perhaps be more successful in hiB search for a weathercock editor, or a weathercock speaker, if he looked a little nearer home.

DEUNICENNIISS.—WIIIIAM Atkinson was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly on the 31st October. ALLEGSD CRUELTY.—Frederick Winniugton was charged with having cruelly ill-treated a horse on the 22nd October, but the case was dismissed. ALLEGED DRUNICENNESS.—George Hall, a member of the Lamm Local Board, WAS charged with having been drunk and incapable on the Ist November at Lymm. P.C. Dutton stated that on the day named, which WaS a Sunday tee Saw the defendant about a quarter past six o'clock in the evening staggering about the road very drunk. He went in the direction of his own house, but on the way fell down lute a ditch. He (the officer) took him up and told him he would be reported. Defendant was in a Iseastly state of drunkenness. and people who were going out to church cried " shame" at him.—Mr. Hall denied having been drunk, and said that when he fell, he fell over a stone. In outer to prove that he was Bober he produced a certificate from Dr. Gailiinore. The Bench, ho‘rever, stated that this could not be taken as evidence, but offered to adjourn the case that Dr. Gallirnore might be subpoeaed. Mr. Hall agreed to this, and the case was accordingly adjourrhd till the next court day. PUBLICANS SUMMONED. Fanny Winstanley, of the Nag's Head Inn, Lynsm' was summoned for having refus, d to serve a Met of whisky to Sergeant Yearsley, on the 27th October. The case was dismissed.—Joseph McCreade, of the Church Inn, Lymm, was also summoned for having sold a pint of whisky which was adulterated with four per 'cent. of water. He was fined 58 and costs, Vs, but his licence was not endorsed. A CARELESS awrien.—Robert Rustige, of Altrincham, was charged with having been asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart, on the 31st October, at Lymm. He was ordered to pay the costs, us 6d. GAME TRESPASS. Thomas Miller and Joseph Miller, two youths, were charged with having trespassed in seerch of game on the 11th of October, at Thelwall, on land in the occupation of Thomas Cook. John Hankinson, gamekeeper, prosecuted on behalf of Mr. P. Stube. He stated that on the Sunday morning he saw the defendants beating the field and hedges with two dogs. They had been warned before. The defendants said they had been hunting after rats. They were each ordered to pay the gusts of the matinees, 5s ffd each. Ceara! FOR DAMAGES —James Barker. of Grapprnhail, thrashing-michine proprietor, claimed £9 lie as damagps against John Shaw for having left his work without notice in August. Defendant did not appear. Mr. B ulcer said be had engaged the defendant to diive his thrashing mach" at 19s a week all the year round. After defendant had been in his employ a week he left without notice, and thereby caused the damage claimed owing to the thrashing machine not being worked for the next four days. An order was made for the defendant to pay £3 16s. ASSAULTING A WIFE.—John Lee, a blacksmith and furian'cutter, Lymm, was charged with having assaulted his wife, Emily Lee, on the 15th November. Complainant said that her husband on the occasion referred to was tipsy, and knocked her about the house. He also threatened to put her out of the way. As defendant did not appear, a warrant for his apprehension was granted. SENT TO AN INDUSTRIAL ScßOOL.—Elizabeth Philips, a widow living at Lymm, was summoned for not having sent her son, John Edward Wakefield, regularly to school. It was stated that the lad said he would never go to school, and his mother had no control over him. He was sent to an industrial school. ALLEGED lIEFT.—Mary Ann Platt, of Lymut, was charged with having stolen a shawl, the property of Mary Jackson, and Ann Platt was charged with having received the same knowing it to hare been stolen. The case was dismissed without having been gone into.

WARRINGTON ELECTION NOTES. There a 4 a considerable number of people who can hardly believe there is such.a thing as a Conserved. tive working-man, and if- they are brought round to that belief.they can never clearly account for the phenomenon. The most promising way of explaining it is that such a ECULL must be imperfectly acquain- ted with the histpry of the two parties, with their ' behaviour towards Ms ONVIi class in particular, and, indeed, that his knowledge of things in general ie hazy and uncertain. This way of meeting the difficulty is to some extent supported by a short dialogue which took place at the Conservative meeting on Monday, between two "real Conserva- tive working-men.' As Dr. Mackie was coming into the room, said one—" It's th' first time he's been here this election; he's feighting Mr. Gladstone in Midlothian." "Nay, he's not," said a better in. formed comrade, who had evidently reached the tte plus ultra of a Conservative working-man's know- ledge of geography and politics, "he's feighting at Monro. By-the-bye where is Monro ? Dr. Mackie preached a characteristic discourse at the Conservative meeting on Monday from the text, "Dr. Mackie in Scotland." Of course it would have been unreasonable to expect him, to digress to any very large extent from this all-absorbing theme, but still he might, considering the circum-• stances under which he spoke, have given a word of encouragement to Sir Gilbert and his friends. The doctor has been out of Warrington lately, and, having had the advantage of watching the local contest from a distance he has evidently come to 'he conclu- sion that the chances of Sir Gilbert are past pray- ing for. By the way, the doctor does not seem to expect to be much troubled with Parliamentary duties after the election is over, as he promised to ,give his "working-men friends" an evening's enter- tainment about Scotch "heckling:' The inhabitants of Blacko, the village visited by Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttleworth on Tuesday even- ing, have good occasion for remembering the "good old Tory days." At a recent Liberal meeting in the place one of the oldest residents stated that about 40 years ago there was only one wedding dress for young women, This was made of calico, and was used at almost all the weddings, the people being too poor to purchase even a cotton dress for their own marriages. This dress went the round of the village in those "palmy days of Protection," his- own wife wearing it on the occasion of their nuptials. Another incident mentioned as having occurred in the same *division, and not far from BlaclfO, shows a striking contrast in the condition of the working-classes, even in these depreSsed times, with that of their parents or grandparentS when the Protection laws were in full operation. Whilst a flmily were engaged at their mid-day , meal—which, like their breakfast and tea, for in Protectionist times slippers were too great a luxury to be afforded by the bulk of the working classes,• consisted of porridge—a sharp knock Caine to the door. The father told one of his children to answer the knock, but the youth was too busily employed, in satisfying the cravings of 'nature to attend to the injunction. It Was, however, repeated, and the boy, whilst endeavouring to keep pace with hie brothers and sisters, replied, " Nay, if I do, I shall , not get my share o' th' porridge.' Thereupon the father cried out, "spoons up," and all spoons were kept out of the porridge dish until the door had • been attended to. As soon, as thelad returned the father gave the order "spoons down," and the assault on the contents of the dish was recommen- ced with renewed vigour. Such are sonie of the' incidents which are being recounted in this district, and vElliCh represent, in no exaggerated form, the condition of the working people in the neighbour- hood before the repeal of the obnoxious Corn Laws. —Preston Guardian.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, Councillor Greening, and Mr. R. Garnett. MISCELLANEOLS —The following were dealt with for drtmkenness :—Arthur O'Brien, in James-street, on Satur- day, discharged; Mary Ann Leech, at the Police Station, dismissed ; George Brooks, in Corporation-street, on Sat- urday night, fined 5s and costs ; James Roan, in Dial- strvet, fined 5s and chats ; Bartholomew McKenna, in Roftl-street, on 6 h the met, fined 59, including costs ; Robert Dakin, at Market-gate, on the Ohs inst, dismissed.— Mary Park was fined is for wheeling a coal truck an the footpath in Bank-street, on the Pth inst ; Mary Faring- ton, for allowing the chimney of her house to be on fire, was finad Is.—Jratrick Winskey was ordered to find sureties for his gsod behavour, or go to gaol for 14 days, he having been found guilty of using threats to his mother. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES—Mr. George Riley appeared to prosecute in the following, cases :—Jarnes Sharp, turner, Blackhurst-street, dismissed ; John Cartwright, tanner, Wright-street, fined 2s 131; Henry Bennett, labourer, Gas- ken- street, case adjourned for a month ; Thomas Clark, Stephen-street, fined 5s ; Thomas Urmson, factory hand. Crossley-street, fined 5s ; William Lawrenson, forgeman, Winwick-street, fined 5s ; Peter Cain, Turner-street, lined 5e ; John Graham. labourer, Winwick-street, fined la ; Mary Gosling, lady help, Warburton-street, boy ordered to Ship " WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough and Alderman
Hole.

MISCELLNNEOGS —Joseph Betley, for refusing to perform his work when a casual inmate of the vagrant ward of the Workhouse. was sent to prison for 14 days.—John Horan, for using threats towards his wife, was bound over to keep the peace for six months. PILFERING BOYS.—Thomas Troy, Matthias Woods, Thos. Knockton, Ralph Woods, and Beth Naylor, hops, were chargtd with stealing a quantity of apples, value 61, from a greengrocer's shop kept by Mrs. Matthews, in Winwick• street.—Troy, who had previously been in trouble, was sttt to prison for a month, to be followed by five years' detention in a reformatory, and the other lads were ordered to recsive twelve strokes each with the birch rod.

THEFT or LEAD.—Albert Barlow, carter, late in the em- ploy of Mr. Henry Barber, coal dealer and contractor, was charged with stealing 106 lbs. of old lead, value Ss, the pro- perty of Mr. Barber. He had disposed of the lead to a marine-store dealer. There was EH previous conviction against prisoner, who has a wife and family, and he was allowed the option of a fine, Ll and costs, in default to go to prison for a month. MISCELLXNEOTTS.—Harry Charnlev, a boy of eleven years of age, was summoned by Frank Dwyer, another boy, for assaulting him. at Latchford, on the 17th inst. Complain- ant alleg•ed that defendant threw a thick piece of glass at him, which struck him on the nose. Defendant was ordered to be kept in custody until evening and pay the costs.— Ann Welsby was summoned for using malicious threats to Annie Lee on the 16th met; she was ordered to pay costs and be bned over to be of good behaviour for six months. —Edward Thomas, for neglecting to send his children to School was, on the information of Mr. Shearer, fined 101.— William Thomason, summoned in respect to one chil.kr was fined 55..

GREAT LIBERAL MEETLNG AT WARRINGTON. SPEECHES OF MR. McMINNIES AND MR. W. , CROSFIELD, &c.

On Wednesday evening a crowded and er.nthusi- astic Liberal meeting was held in the Public Hall. Something like an hour before the commencement of the meeting the hall was filled in every part, and during the period of waiting several political songs were sung with much heartiness and effect. Amongst the songs sung were "March, Boys, March," "Auld Lang Syne," Ste., Mr. G. Wallington being leader and Mr. Pearson presiding at the organ. In the in- tervals between songs the irrepressible Mr. Diggle was to the fore, and addressed the meeting on various topics with his well-known coherence and eloquence. The chuir was taken by Mr. J, G. McMinnies, and there were also on the platform Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P., the Hon. J. W. Mansfield, ROT. E. Lloyd Jones, Mr. J. Crosfield, J.P., Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P., Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., Rev. J. Youge, Rev. J. Howell Jones, Rev. E. Moore, Mr. F. R. Roberts, Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., H. Roberts (secretary) and numerous others. Several ladies were also present. The Czarnmen said Mr. Roberts would reaa two letters of apology far the non-attendaace of those who were expec- ted there that night. Mr. H. ROBERTS then read the following letters : Pray Castle, Amtleside. Nov. 7,1885.-50 y near Crosfield,— If I could I most gladly would come to help you per- sonally I heartily with you sticce.s. But I have meetings fixed, I fear, for every avail Asia day to the election. I have a hard fight here, but am hopeful.—Yours ever sin- cerely. PARSER HEseCtiELL. Oakhill Park. 14th Nov.. 1835.—ljear r. Orosfield.—l am very sorry, but my advanced years torbid me attending putlic meetings. 1 was constrained to make an exception in Samuel Smith's case and fem bound to attend at almost any risk, and I was not s,rry to have the opp triunity of stating before a large and influential meeting of the electors that the political ophoons I had formed in ear, life, and which I had consistently retained for more than half a cent u,y, and my ad- herence to the tibe,a, party was as firm still on on the day I was first competent to torm a decided political op Mon. There are few now liv ng who have had greater experience than I have had of the acts and conduct of the Liberal party in refe-- ence to Roman 0 .ahotics. and I know every privilege we p)s- stss, worth hsving, we owe to the Liberal party—(loud ap- plause)—ard the deep store of pr vitude which I tee towards them is, I hope and treat, thoroughly impressed on the minds and limits of all right-minded Catholics. (loud applause ) Cordially ishing vou success.•-1. am, Yours faithfully. Joillf YATES —William Co ,field. Esq. The Cerarnmeet said he had to apologise for the ab- sence of Mr. Peter Ryl tnds. He was so much engaged at Burnley that they could not press him to come here, es- pecially as he wrote to sty that he Lad an engagement, which was by far the most important he had had in Burnley during the present election. He (the chairman) had ne doubt they. all regretted Mr. Rylands' absence, but at the same time he thought they would understand that Mr. Rylands' first duty was to his own constituency. (Hear, hear.) Passing from that there was one matter about which he thought he was expected to say something, and that matter was the fixing of the day of polling in that borough. (Hear, hear.) Some three or four weeks ago he was spoken to by a large employer of labour in that town, who told him that it was important that they should have a Saturday fixed as a day of polling. He (the chairman) said he had no doubt ea all that both parties would be consulted in reference to the day of polling, and that he would bear the recommenda- tion in mind. He had been mistaken in supposing that both parties would be consulted in connection with the fixing of the day of polling—(" Shame t') —and the first intimation he understood that the Own had that Tueeday, the 24th, was fixed was derived from a local newspaper. (" Shame.") He did not know until Tuesday the 11th that the day had been fixed, because the reading of newspapers just now was rather a heavy business, and if there were any newspapers that they had to emit reading—(laughter)—well, they had to judge for themselves which they would omit. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He did not know until Tuesday that the day had been fixed. So convinced was he that Tuesday was about the worst day, considering the interests of the workmen and employers, for the ingenuity of any man to have devised, that he asked for ars interview with the Tarn Clerk and the Mayor. On the following day they met the Town Clerk and the Mayor and the representa- tives of the other party, and after arguing a good deal, and finding in the first instance that the authorities of the town believed that Saturday was a very bad day indeed, and that they could not answer for the peace of the town if Saturday were 'chosen. ("Oh, oh.") Finding that the authorities had made up their minds on that point they pleaded for Friday—(hear, hear)—but they were equally unsuccessful there, and he must say they cam. away from that meeting believing that Tuesday was inevitable. But after leaving he found that the feeling was so strong in Warrington that Tuesday was a bad day that he attempted again to get it altered. They sought another interview, and ultimately it ended in their meeting the Mayor and the representatives of Sir Gilbert Greenall at the Town Hall. They argued in favour of I Friday again, and against Tuesday, but they came away having entirely failed in the object that they sought. If anybody said that they had any other purpose in view than that of saving the money .of the workpeeple and the em- ployers they said that thing which was not accurate. (Hear, hear.) If anybody said that they consented to Tuesday it was not true ; they submitted to Tuesday be- cause they had no choice. (liear, hear.) They consented in the sense that a man consented to receive a flogging. (Laughter, and applause.) Ile took it because he could not help it, but he slid not consent to it. (Laughter.) They took Tuesday, because they could not help it, but they never consented to it, and to that day they thought Tues- day was about the worst that could have been chosen. (Hear, hear.) Passing from that subject for a moment to another, he understood that a meeting was held on the pre- vious night in that town, and that their Catholic fellow voters were exhorted to give their votes to the other aide. (A voice : "We shan't," and loud applause.) What ! Catholics join Orangemen to support a Tory? (Hear, bear, and applause, and a voice: "Never.") He protested against that unnatural, that unholy alliance. (Loud ap- plause.) But be did not believe in it. (Hear, hear.) Irish Catholics in this town to his certain knowledge for 40 years bad been loyal to the Liberal party, and he did not believe that at this day they were going to break that allegiance. (A Voice: "We have more sense." and applause.) Especially he did not believe they were going to break that allegiance in reference to a Tory candidate' who all his life had been more or less connected with Orangemen, and who, when the chief, or one of the chiefs, of the Orange party, proposed that the convents of the United Kingdom should be put under an inspection voted for that inspection. He (the c-)airman) had three nieces in Catholic convents, and he said that that motion of Mr. Newdegate was a base insult to the ladies that had the superintendence in those institutions and a base insult to the parents and guardians of the young ladies who had placed them in that institution. (I-tear, hear.) No! he had no fear of the Catholic vote. (Loud applause.) Nothing had been done on the previous night to destroy what he bad called the allegiance of the Catholic party to: the Liberal party, and they might depend upon it that nothing was said that was at all likely to damage the interests of the Liberal party in that borough. (Aleplause.) He understood that at the meeting referred to it was stated to them what had happened in the House of Commons since the present Government Come into power a few weeks ago, bat what about the 40 or 50 years that most of tbern could remember of the Tory action in reference to the Catholics. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) There had been nothing brought forward in favour of the repeal of disabilities of the Catholic that bad not been opposed in his lifetime by the Tory party (Hear, hear.) Why, Mr. O'Connell had to fight against the Tory party all his life. (Applause.) Oh, for one hour of O'Connell! (Loud applause.) They should not be in the state they were now if O'Connell lived. (Hear, hear.) But he had no doubt that everybody who had been loyal to the Liberal party hitherto would be loyal here- after. (Hear, hear.) And he had no doubt at all that those efforts which were made by a desperate party to redeem a beaten cause would only stimulate them to renewed exertions so that next Tuesday they should find tbemselvesin the posi- tion that they had occupied for the last five years—an unassailable and victorious party in the town. (Loud ap- Iplause.)

Mr. W. CLIOSFIELD, who was received with enthusiastic cheering, again and again renewed, said his first word that night must be acword of condolence. He could not forget that that afternoon Warrington had lost her member. The Queen had that afternoon dispensed with the services of the members of Parliament—(bear, hear)—and if he was accu- rately informed, at that moment there was not a member Of Parliament existing in England. Warrington had lost one to whom she had been in the habit of looking up to for many years. (Hear, hear.) One who had represented her in the House of Commons with very great distinction, and one who had faithfully represented their views In that honourable House. (Hear, bear.) He felt sure that they would agree with him in giving expression to his feeling of regret, but he also felt that wherever their late member was he would be respected by them as a worthy representa- tive of Liberalism—(applause)—and that as long as he lived, and wherever he lived, he would still Le a prominent War- rington Liberal. (Applause.) During the many opportu- nities which he (Mr. Crosfield) had had of addressing them be had spoken upon a great many subjects, and they now came verwnear to the close of that contest for what was now the vacant seat. He thought be had spoken upon al- most every subject that might be considered a burning question, but a whisper reached him that he bad not spoken about trade. He was under the impression that he had said a good deal about trade, but some ptople did not seem to have heard what he said He had enlarged upon the merits of Free Trade and the demerits of Fair Trade lie bad spoken from time to time of the Royal Commission on Trade and the much-maligned members of the Liberal party who we -eke Ito take a seat upon that Commission. Well, sonn• o em were perhaps aware that the Commis- sion, havin,„ commenced its labours, bad issued a report. The report was only a brief one, but it con• tamed a great deal of matter which was vett, well worth attention. One of the most prominent witnesses before the Commission was a gentleman named Mr. Crow, who was asked to give his opinion in regard to the depres- sion of trade in other parts of the world than England. in his evidence he said "I have every reason to think that the depression we find in England exists in almost every other Kuropean country. It exists in France, it exists in Bel- gium, and it exists in Germany in dift-rent degrees. In k.leti case there is depression." (Hear, hear.) Well, let them look to the great country of America, which so many

He then proposed "That this meeting perhaps they would prefer that Mr. Gladstone should be pledges itself to use every legitimate effort to secure the given the task of putting the pinnacle on the structure,of Irish redress which he had largely helped to build up." , triumphant return of William Crosfield, Esq., J.P." (Cheers.) structure. (Load applause.) There was another subject . I . . . _ . . . . ..

upon which he thought his utterances had been very clear, but upon which some of his friends told him they wished to hear him speak again. That was with regard to educe- , tion and religious education in schools. (Applause.) lie had to say claiming—he said it humbly—to be a religious man himself—(load applause)—he had no sympathy with the exclusion of religion from denominational schools. (Hear, hear.) He recognised the value of denominational schools. During the last 15 years they had made great strides in the matter of education, and they were proud of the success they had achieved: Before the existing Bdueation Act came into existence there was only 1,250,000 attending their schools, but now they looked with satisfao4 tion to the fact that there were 5,000,000. (Applause.) That was a great thing to have achiexed, but he believed that nothing like that result could have been attained if it had not been for the co-operation of the denominational school managers throughout the land. (Applause.) But to put it briefly, and to put it so that it could be clearly understood he would state his opinion to be that he would oppose compulsory attendance of Catholic children at any school where their religion was not taught, and he would piernote an inquiry into the working of the existing educa- tion which Cardinal Manning had asked fer with a view to have all elementary schools put upon a perfectly equal footing. (Applause.) And now to pass to another subject which he had not alluded to in public. They were twitted from lime to time with the great enormity of spending £100,000,000 in the present year. Sir Gilbert Greene!' in his address—(hisses)—do not hurt his opponent, he was unfortunately laid up ill at borne, and he thought they ought all to treat him with consideration. (A Voice : " We will beat him," and laughter.) Sir Gilbert Greenall lacing more Tory than his Tory followers, he supposed, had said in his address that the expenditure this year was more , than £100,000,000, and his chairman, Mr. Reynolds, talked of the last Government having left a legacy of expenditure of £100,000,000. He (Mr. Crosfield) supposed if he were to , talk for an hour they probably would say at the end of it that they knee., more about it than he did, and perhaps some of them would go the length of saying he did not eperk the truth. But the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir M. Hicks-Beach, in alluding to that question of the gigantic expenditure—and he (Mr. Crosfeld) did not wish kr a moment to palliate the fact that it was infinitely larger than the expenditure of this country ought to be— khear, hear)—but Sir M. Hicks-Beach, speaking of that question, brushed the thing on one side, and said "Of course no one professes to say the expenditure was really , £100,000,000." (Laughter.) Yet their friends were still going about saying it was. Mr. Childers had explained that , the real expenditure was only £77,880,000. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Crosfield) believed their party were the economists, . as Mr. Howes—(applause)—told them a few days ago. He showed that the Liberal party managed the affairs of the nation more economically than the other party when dealing only with the necessary expenditure and leaving out the extras which had caused the large expenditure. They *were exceedingly glad to have the help of three new con- verts to economy on their side, but in locking at converts one generally looked back at their record, and when he found his honourable opponent denouncing the Liberal party for their extravagance he could not fail to remember a certain occasion when a gentleman whom they hoped to have there that night was very much impressed with the vast expenditure, and he introduced a series of resolutions to the House of Commons. Mr. Peter Rylands—(applause) —moved—and he wculd give the date so that his opponent's memory might not fail him—(laughter)—on the 28th April, 1879, four resolutions upon which votes were taken. This was one of the resolutions :—" That the taxes required to meet the present expenditure impede the operations of agri- culture and manufacture and dimtnished the funds for the employment of labour in all branches of productive in- dustry, thereby tending to produce pauperism and crime, anti adding to the general and local burden of the people." (Applause.) When Mr. Rylands moved that resolution the expenditure wail £81,000,000 and Sir Gilbert Greenall was in the House at the time and what did beds 2 He voted against it. (Hear, hear.) In commencing that contest he (Mr. Crosfield) expressed a wish that all personal considera- tions should be left put of the question. He expressed the hope that he should be able to treat his opponent simply as the representative of a political party, and be believed that he had adhered to that determination. (Hear, hear.) At any rate his own conscience did not convict him of having trespassed in any sense. (Applause.) He himself had been attacked as a man of business. Statements had been made about the tirm with which he was connected, statements which bad been false in their inception and ',alkali had been malicious in their results. (Hear, hear.) He should have been glid to have closed that contest without a reference to the commercial position of his oppanent, but he had himself chosen in ,a speech which he made in the North East ward on Thursday night last to make some- allusion to his business relations. He spoke in this sense "Let them have trade; straightforward, righteous trade if they could get it—(laughter)—and he thought .it was the bounden duty of all of them, according to their means and power, to do their best righteously to assist in returning trade He was speaking as a tradesman, and to them as tradesmen. He never learnt, and never would learn--(laugh- ter)-to regard the working-man as anything else than a kind of section or party belonging to the same trade as himself. (Loud laughter.) He believed that capital had its rights, and he believed as firmly also that labour had it rights. He believed capital was only good and useful when it was

The Rev. R. FILCHER, 8.A., seconded the resolution. He , had the honour, he said, to minister to a congregation in that town that had maintained for over 200 years an un- broken religious life, founded on the search after and the spread of civil and religious liberties all the world over— (applause)—and be had always belonged, both by sympathy and circumstances, to that party which had continuously and steadfastly, and with set purpose followed after peace, retrenchment, and reform. (Applause.) They had not always gained what they sought. Peace was not always possible in a large country like this, or where the Jingoes • had an opportunity of reaching to power. Retrenchment was not always possible where "a spirited foreign policy" I was able to contract debt, but which it Was not spirited j enough to pay. (Applause.) Reform was not possible in I the face of a great party which had steadfastly, con- tinuously, and with a set purpose, set their faces against all reform' and where they bad been forced to give way, they sent the reforms that had been embodied through Partia- -1 ment maimed and mutilated where they could not he crushed. (Applause.) Mr. Disraeli long ago spoke of the Conservative Government of his day as " an organised hypocrisy." An organised hypocrisy they were to the present day, for they gave with their right hand only to take away with their left. Be need only turn to what had that night been said to show that the Tories of that town bad been at their old game, harassing the people, and harassing them by appointing Tuesday instead of Saturday or Friday, as they might have done, as the. polling day. Everything, in fact, that they put forward was a shameful sham. He had no doubt that the gentlemen the chairman spoke of expreseed their deep sympathy with the working men, and their desire to save his pocket to the best of their ability, but they fixed the Tuesday all the same. The Tory democrat for instance,.wbat a sham he wan. The hands, ne doubt were the hands of the democratic Esan. but the voice was ! the well-known voice of the wily Tory Jacob. (Applause.) "I understand," said Lord Disraeli in a pamphlet he issued some years ago, "I understand a Tory." That was more thaa be (the speaker) did. He understood a Radical, but a democratic aristocrat he did not comprehend. (Laughter and cheers.) Lord Randolph Churchill—(hisses)—had bettered the instrnctions of his master, and be pieced to- I gether the aristocrat and the . democrat. The Tories were great at religion. (A voice: sometimes.) The Church was al- ways in danger, and they were always there t 6 protect good mother Church. Well, surely one would think that such eminent patrons of religion such patrons that they sent her forth with the Government stamp on—one would have thought, such eminent patrons would know that in stitching on the strong democratic cloth to the rotten rags of Toryism, their religion ought at least to have warned them. They had, they knew, started Fair Trade, which meant that they and he were to pay to keep up the rents— (hear, bear,)—and the landed aristocracy. He said that when they put theptrong cloth on to the rotten cloths of Toryism their religion should have taaght them that the rent always became worse. (Laughter and applause.) He put Fair Traders amongst the other shams of the Tory party. They had another Tory sham in their midst. If they looked at Mr. Gladstone's speech of the previous day, they would see he was speaking of newspapers, and referred to the, what should be call them—the temporising newspapers. They knew something about temporising newspapers is that town. (Laughter.) He said that all these shams, these 1 Tory Democrats, these Fair Traders, and these temporising 1 newspapers were on the dead level of sham organised hypo- 1 cilia', and only fit to COXIB from the brain of—he was glad that he had to go to a foreign language to express what he meant—only fit to come trom the brain of a Machiavelli. (Applause and laughter.) He supported Mr. Crosfield with all his heart, because he wanted to be their representative and not their delegate. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry that the crotchet-mongers were abroad—he had been deluged with pamphlets and lists of questions that he had been re- quested to bother various candidates with, but he had put them all on one side. He should be afraid of pes- tering them lest the candidate should remind him that he wanted to be a representative and not a delegate, and he was afraid that another candidate would gently insinuate that if the questioner had read his speeches and studied his address as he should have done, the putting of the ques- tions would have been quite needless trouble both to the questioner and the questioned. But he was indignant to see these people trundling their little petty go-cart in the way of the four great omnibuses which the Liberals said they must drive. (Applause.) He was indignant at seeing, when they stood on the threshold of one of the greatest fight?, and one of the greatest causes that England had had to face since 1832, to see what damage the disestablishment question had caused. The Tories were keen enough to see the damage that such a question, mooted now, would cause, and they were making the most of it. He did not believe, nor did he think any Liberal believed, that Mr. Gladstone was wrong whea he said that that question was far removed into the vista of years. He supported Mr. Crosfield because he had read his speeches, end had heard him speak and had studied his address, and when he had been in Liverpool he had asked of his friends there, upon whose judgment he could rely—who had worked with Mr. Crostield on public questions, and had every ~pportunity of studying him closely—and they all assured him that in all points on which he had a right to look narrowly to the man who wanted to represent them in Par- liament, the scrutiny would be perfectly satisfactory. (A p- • planse.) For these reasons, and for others, he was there
that night, as he hoped to be on other occasions, to support Mr. Crosfield's candidature with both his voice and his vote. (Applause.)

The Hon. J. W. MANSFIELD next addressed the meeting. After a reference to Mr. Croefield he remarked that the Tories were rather fond of saying that the Liberals were anxious to look forward to the future, but were very' much ashamed of the past. The Liberals had a future to look forward to, and they had a definite programme laid before the country by Mr. Gladstone, who mid that they must first of all have the procedure et the House of Com- mons improved so that they, might be able to pass the measures which were necessary for the welfare of the community. After detailing advantageous measures passed by the Liberal party, the speaker asked them to place Mr. Crosfield at the head of the poll, and their victory would be a trumpet note to the whole of the Liberal party in the kingdom, and would give them encouragement for the battle that they wowld have to fight. (Applause.) The Rev. LLOYD JONES, in an interesting addrecs, in the course of which he was repeatedly cheered, said that he hoped Mr. Filcher did not consider that the disestablish- ment of the Church in Wales was a crotchet. (Hear, hear.) He thought that no Liberal would be so weak-kneed or so unjust as to tie round the neck of Wales a church that only three ent of ten want. As regarded the English Churcii, they might do what they liked with it, and without much loss to Wales they could send all the parsons to help them. He was always glad to come to Warrington, because it was there that he had his political baptism. It was in Warring- ton where be plunged into the waters of political life, and he might say that there was nothing that he had done dur- ing his life ter which his conscience mere applauded him than his entering into political life and becoming a political parson. (Applause.) His conception of religion was first fair play in this world. He was not willing to speak only of , a heaven beyond the clouds, but he wanted to help people to I have fair play in this world below. (Applause.) He tho- I roughly believed in their candidate—(applause)—and was certain that the more they saw of Mr. Crosfield the more they would respect him. (Hear, hear.) He was exactly the type of man that would be required in the House of Commons more and more every year. (Applause.) He had not the slightest doubt but that they would return Mr. Crosfield. He was not prepared for a moment to think that when they returned Mr. McMinnies—(cheersj—it was all because of his genial face and liberal hand, or that it was on account of the power of his wit mid oratory. No, he believed that however much was the personal nflueace of Mr. McMinnies, their conversion was not to Mr. McMinnies but to Liberalist. (Applause.) He had no doubt that Mr. Crosfield on his being returned would show that they had elected him as they elected M. McMin- nies, on the ground of personal and political fitness. (Ap- plause.) They were DOW entering upon what he might term the third era of the political history of this country. The first era was that of government by the few for the benefit of the few. That was Toryism and it was dead. (Laughter and applause.) Nay, he might the better say that Toryism had lost its reputation and had become politi- cally bankrept. " Toryism going down the street one day met an innocent, honest, genuine young man, called Demo- cracy, and said to him ' Will you come into partnership with me. That will float me for my name stinks politi- cally in the history of England. Your name means liberty, fraternity, come into partnership.' " If Democracy ever became a partner with bankrupt Toryism, Toryism would , become hideous to the nostrils of the country. There was also the Whig era—government by the few for the benefit of the maey. That was dying of consumption—laughter I and applause)—and its days were numbered. He did not I want to hasten the day, but must look at thins as they were. The day to govern the country by a few members I ef a certain class had gone, and now they stood upon the threshold of the political millenium of this country— government by the people for the welfare of the people. (Loud applause.) He could sing "God save the Queen " as well as any Tory could, he could sing "God save the Queen and the mon- archy " as well as any man in the room, but if he were a poet and could make a song, he should like to make one in which " Parliament, save the pence" should always be sung at the end of "God save the Queen." (Ap- plause.) When he looked into that wonderful almanac— the financial reform almanac—he believed that if an honest Tory were to read it through he would become a Radical in less than 24 hours. (Applause.) He looked at the expen- diture connected with the Crown in this country. He should think their beloved Queen was more bamboozled than any other woman in the land, with the retainers given to various persons: The Duke of Weetmineter had £2,500 for being Master of the Horse, and £Boolor his Becretary, who did the work. Then there was a Master of the Buck- heunde. 'What did they care about the huckhourids ? (Laughter and applause.) Did they ever hear of such art abominable piece of class legislation as to pay £2,000 a year so that a certain number of flunkeys from Luedon should run after the buckhounds-(renewed laughter and ap- plause)—when there were so many empty cupboards in the country, and when there were hundreds and thousands of far- mers who could not pay their rents. He asked thome who went to Parliament to take a knife with them and to cut away those miserable expenses. (Applause ) The stability of the Throne did not depend upon them. How to govern the country more cheaply would be the first question, and the second would be how to bridge over the enormous chasm that now existed between luxury on the one hand and biting poverty on the other. That tremendous chasm between triumphant wealth and poverty was neither the ordination of a good God or of a wise man. (Applause.) How then to increase the income of the country ? The laws affecting the land required altering. He had been speaking to a large number of farmers and had asked them what really was the state of agriculture, and their unanimous testimony was that for every 15s that they could possibly make, their liabilities were 208. The good old book said that the land was given to the children of men, but some people said it was given to chil- dren of the aristocracy. (Laughter and applause.) They should bring about a change whereby there should be no faecy land as long as there were people looking for bread. Having spoken of the large tracts of land devoted to the purposes of deer forests Mr. Jones proceeded to say that he had always been on the side of Irishmen. (Applause.) He had even offended some people in Warrington because they thought that he was too much in love with the Irish. If the Irish, he said, allied themselves with those who had been their enemies as long as Ireland had been under the control of England, they would, firs{ of all, be very ungrate- ful for past favours. He would rather have a gift, if it was the same, from an honest man tkan from a hypocrite. (Applause.) The policy of the Tories, so far as Ireland was concerned, had been to resist everything—to bind the Irish down—and now they wanted the Irish vote. They could only serve their own country by being true to their prin- cipleit and they could not be true to their principles if they sacrificed tkemselves to the Tories. (Applause.) The speaker then asked the sympathy of hie audience for the Welsh, who, he said, were fighting the battle of emancipa- tion from landlordism. He asked for justice for the "Land . of Jones." • (Applause.)

Mr. Joine CROSFIELD, who was loudly cheered, rose to Propose a vote of thanks to the Chairman. They had, he said, often before been indebted to Mr. McNlionies, but never more so than that night. (Applause.) Mr. Jones said that there were some things that made his blood boil. There were some things that made his (the speaker's) blood boil. It was injustice and the want of fair play. He was going to speak very plainly: The Liberal party in Warrington was bigger than the Tory party,, and deserved as much consideration, and be said that the Mayor of Warrington had not abowu fair play to the Liberal party. (Applause.) At every previous election the Mayor of the borough had consulted the representatives of the Liberal as well as the Tory party as to what day would be meat convenient for the election. (Hear, hear.) That had not been done this time. (A Voice: " Shame.") The first notice that they received of the election appeared in the Warring tom Guardian. of Saturday week. He wanted to know who gave that date, which would not have been published without proper information. That information had come from the Town Clerk's office. The Mayor of Warrington fixed the date, and it was decided before Mr. McMinnies, himself, or the election agent, were asked to go to the Town Clerk's office to discuss when the day of elec- tion should be. What did they find when they got there? I They used arguments in favour of Friday, knowing that the great mass of the labour electors in Warrington would rather have Friday than Tuesday. (Applause.) - If held on a Tuesday a loss would be caused both to men and employers. It would be a very serious loss to the owners of Hallam Forge, and a very groat loss to the men who worked there. He was sorry that these men should be compelled to lose their wages. They found that everything that they said was useless. Mr. Sylvanus Reynolds had got the ear a the Mayor, they had arranged the day before hand, and any argu- ment that they, could they might 85 well have urged to a milestone. It was said that when they left the office of the the Town Clerk they had agreed on Tuesday. They were like man, as the chairman had said, who submitted to a dogging because he could not help it. They disagreed with the date then, and they disagreed with it now. (Applause.) He saidthat the Tories had concocted this thinking that the Liberal voters and their captains would be fastened in on Tuesday. That was their little game, bnt it would take a good deal bigger man than the Mayor of Warrington to do that. (Applause.) His opinion was that instead of the Tory pant benefiting by this arrangement they would find that the exasperation and indignation that had been excited amongst the Liberals would be so great that it would really bring more electors to the Liberal poll than would have gone before. His opinion was that the Tcries would be thrashed with their own stick, as they deserved to be. He was not the man to speak in this manner unless be believed it co be true, or to ask for something that was not fair and just. They had a right, as representing the Liberal party, to use their arguments in favour of Friday, because it would have saved the working-men a great deal of wages and would also have saved the employers a great loss of money. (Applause.) Those were arguments that any Mayor of any borough in England should listen to. (Ap- plause.) It was not fair, or just, that they ebauld be treated in that way, just because the Tory potty thought that if it was fixed on Tuesday the working-men would be fastened in the works and would not be able to vote. Mr. Reynolds spoke in this way—" Act up to the spirit of the Reform Act." Mr. Reynolds was a friend of his, but he thonght that it was a little cheeky for him to talk in that way. He said the "Act now leaves the poll open until eight o'clock at night, so that working-men could vote between six and eight o'clock, and have no need to leave their work." For all the working-men Liberal electors to remain at work until six o'clock at night and then vote was a physical impossibility. He would venture to advise Mr. Reynolds to "act up to the spirit of the Corrupt Practices
