MR. LEADAM'S CANDIDATURE.

On Saturday evening Mr. I. S. Leadam, who is contesting the Altrinc.ham Division of Cheshire in the Liberal interest, delivered an address at the British School, Altrincham. Mr. C. J. Morris pre- -sided, and he was supported by numerous other gentlemen. Amongst these were Mr. F. W. Grafton, M.P., Mr. George Bowen (mayor of Altrincham), Mr. A. Neild, Profeesor T. D., Hill, the Rev. Horace Hill, Messrs. J. X. Bradbury, J. T. Armitage, William Armitage, jun.', Neville Clegg. Ernest Bellbouse, W. Milne, Jesse Haworth, W. Rigby, Adam Hogg, D. Senior, A. Behrens, C. C. Dunkerley. and Walter Ha- worth. Several ladies, including Mrs. Leadam, also had seats on the platform.—The Chairman having spoken, Mr. F. W. Guarrox, M.P., who was received with cheers, spoke eulogistically of Mr. Leadam, who, he said, was a highly educated man, capable of giving adequate expression to the opinions he held. To some subjects he had devoted ' deep consideration, and was especially an authwity on agricultural topics, which were of great importance to that particular district. Mr. I. S. I,Renett then addressde the meeting. Afte referring to statements made by Mr. Brooks, his opponent, Mr. Leaden pointed out what he esteemed to be the hol- lowness and impracticability of Lord Salisbury's retailia- tory proposals as regarded our trade with foreign nations. The probable effect of such a policy applied to a country like Ppain, instanced by Lord Salisbury, was no criterion to judge by. If we were to embark upon such a policy against any nation in the world it would primarily have to be the United States. What were our commercial relations with America? We imported thence £2,500,000 manufacturers per year while our annual import of food from the States amounted to no less a sum than £100,000,000. Retaliatory duties upon American produce imported into this country would therefore mean a tax upon food; and other indica- tions were not wanting to prove that the Conservative party were endeavouring to lead British workmen unawares te support taxation on the necessaries of life. (Hear, hear.) Without considering in all its bearings the incidence of taxation he (Mr. Leadam) said there was one matter in respect to which a revision was necessary for the benetit of the working-classes. In England only 5 per cent of imperial taxation was levied on laid, as compared with 18 per eent in France, 11 in Prussia, and 17 in Austria. It was not his wish that the farmers, who already had good ground for complaint, should be bur- dened more heavily with local taxation, but those landlords who thought' the country was made wealthy by the " un- earned increment " which the industrial classes created, ought to pay their proper proportion. Working-men had to pay directly or indirectly, while the owners of great estates in the neighbourhood of thriving towns were exempt from rates on ground rents, though the value of their property was added to year after year by the busy populations of the tewne. (" Shame.") The present system of local govern- ment was entirely for the benefit of the aristocracy. The lighting, paving, draining and other work upon which the expenditure of rates took place were properly attended to in so far as rich men's houses were concerned, whereas the homes of the working classes were shrouded in darkness, the paving in front of them was neglected, and for want of proper drainage being provided fevers were apt to be bred there. These unjust knornalles could only be put as end to when all men had an equal voice in matters touched by local government. (Cheers.) A. little attention must be paid to the just rights of human flesh and blood as well as to those rights of pro- perty of which Mr. Brooks was always speaking. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, Mr. Lead= said that Liberalism was the force of the future, the cause was a righteous one, and time was on its side. (Loud cheers.) A resolution pledging the meeting to further Mr.Leadam'e candidature was moved by Mr. A. Bend, seconded by Mr. T. Vernon, supported byMr. J. K. Bradbury, and carried.

MEETING AT HALTON. On Monday evening a public meeting of the elec- tors of Halton was held in the Court Room, Halton Castle Hotel, in support of Mr. J. T. Brunner, the Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division. The room was well filled. Mr. J. N Lello occupied the chair, and on the platform were the candidate, Messrs. B. Kniveton, 'fi". Handley, and 0. Leak. The thulium/LW said he wished to draw attention to a matter which they had undoubtedly seen in the newspapers, and that was the abominable and disgraceful proceedings about that day fortnight at the Conservative meeting in the Public Hall in Runcorn. There were only two or three eye-witnesses of the transaction, and as those present might have only heard the rumours he would briefly allude to the matter, because the report circulated was untrue. It was without the least foundation or the shadow ef a truth. It so happened that a few days before the meeting he (Mr. Lello) asked a friend if he would favour him with a couple of tickets for the Conservative meeting. His friend said he would see the secretary, Mr. Lightburn. and he had not the least doubt that two tickets would be supplied to him. The thkets came, but with the understanding that "Mr. 'Llano must say ncthing at the meeting." Now, it was not his intention to say anything, but to attend the meeting out of curiosity to see hew the Conservatives carried on their I business. So that his good wife might be free from any crush, he went to the meeting an hour before the time an- nounced for commencing. He intended seeing his wife to her seat, and then to leave the meeting for another engage- ment. On entering the hall he told the ticket collector his intentions, and that official told him he would give him his ticket when he returned from the hall. What followed? As soon as be made his appearance in the ante-room ef the hall—when he mentioned the gentleman's name they would know that he was almost capable of any amount of imperti- nence—Mr. Lightburn's son—he was not so familiar with him as to know his Christian name, but he Was a young man with a black moustache--approached him and said he was not to enter. He (Mr. Lello) asked for an explanation, but Mr. Lightburn's son could only retaliate by saying that he was not going to enter that door. They might be sure that he raS taken aback, as any gentleman would be with his wife by his side when he was told he could not enter. fie persisted in having an explanation, and after a good deal of pressure he was told to show his tickets. That was amusing, after he had got so far into the hall. After pressing for a further explanation, he was told that the ladies only could enter by that door, and no gentleman would be permitted to enter. He stated that he wished to see his wife to her seat, and then to leave the hall, but he was told that he was not go- ing to pass that door with his wife. Mr. Lightburn's son then walked from the door, which led him (Mr. Lello) to believe that he had repented of his ungentlemanly conduct. He, therefore made another attempt to take his wife to a seat, but Mr. therefore, son stepped between them and prevented his entrance. At that moment his father came up and was told what had occurred, and he instantly said that Mr. Lello, having given his word tbat he was going out of the hall again, it was 'quite sufficient, and he should be allowed to take his enfe to her seat. Half an hour after- wards, When he had lulficied his appointment, he returned to the ball and entered by the front eatrance, when a party came round and tried to eject him. Tleli WaS very nice polite conduct ! They were now Bitting it ail Oat, in Order to varnish their wicked ways, that Mr. Lello persisted in sitting with the ladies. Such a report was proved to be false by the fact that he bad made every arrangement to leave the hall again after seeing his wife to a seat. He did net think there was a gentleman present who could hold up his hand in favour of such a prooseding as that he had described. A great deal of sympathy had been shown to him even by right-thinking men on the Conserva- tive Bide, and he really believed the Conservative party would lose many votes through it; and he believed that many Conservatives on the day of polling would not record their votes in favour of such conduct. (Hear, bear, and applause.) If the Conservatives made it a part of their programme to engage roughs to assault peaceable citizens, he was not the man to look favourably upon that party who engaged and incited Others to rowdyism. This was not the party qualified to govern the affairs of a nation. He understood that a resolution had been passed at a meeting of Conservatives to engage several strong and stalwart men as " chuckers out "—(laughter)—so that should any pro- minent Liberale make any appearance they were to be ejec- ted. One man.at the meeting, whose name he would not mention, said they were to have a little bit of that—(shak- ing his tist—laughter)—if this party went in for boxing when they were on their haunches, what would they do when they were on stilts? The fact of the position in which he was found that evening was evidence sufficient that he bad no sympathy with Conservative principles. Mr. Lello then dealt with general politics, and urged those pre- sent if they desired peace, prosperity, happiness, progress, to vote straight to a man for Mr. Brunner, who was not only willing but able to fight the battle of the Liberal cause in their interest. (Applause.) Mr. BatiNNEA said he had not come with any set speech, and asked thoee present upon what subject be should ad- dress them. Land was suggested, and Mr. Brunner dealt with that subject. He described how hundreds of years ago the land was held from the King as the representative of 'the nation, under a guarantee that those in possession would maintain an army in the field, a watch in the Tower, and repair the roads and bridges. There were no landowners. There were only landholders, who bad to pay the expenses of the State. In 1682 the House of Commons, every member a landholder from the King, passed, by a majority of two, a , bill abolishing those duties the landholder owed to society 1 and the nation, and they enacted that in lieu thereof in full satisfaction to his Majesty for ever, an excise duty upon beer. (A Voice: " I would put a bit more on that," and laughter.) From that time Parliament enacted one law after another in favour of the men who had then become land- owners, until 1532, when for the first time men who were not landowners got the vote, and since then matters had been slowly mending. The results of these acts had been that four fifths of the land in England belonged to 4,500 persons—('• shame ")—and 1,700 persons held nine tenths ef the land in Scotland. Under these circumstances it was impossible to purchase land at a fair bargain. The can- didate described the iniquities of „the law of dis- tress, and stated that almost everywhere if a far- mer improved his land the landlord charged him rent upon his improvements. These were the con- ditions imposed upon the greatest trade in the country by land owners parliaments. Alluding to the evils of short leases, Mr. Brunner said that in Southport the property was built under leases for 75 years and at the end of that time 999 houses out of every 1,000 would belong to three families. In Southport and other places where short leases obtained, the houses were built guaranteed not to last longer than the lease, and they were not two• years old before the walls began to crack. (Laughter.) There were many houses they could see daylight through. Did they think it a benefit to the country that Jerry houses should be built—(" No no ")—in order simply that people who built them should be robbed of as little as possible by the land owner. (Applause.) In the slums of Liverpool and the worst parts of London nine out of ten houses were the goingpoot or irneao.tvribl i folks whowhalived t in k could t themheysexpectan and dt sank esdfyo; , body and soul as the house sank and sank physically. Hain entered in the house through the roof, and sewer gas came up from below, and the people rotted with rheu- matism and typhoid fever, and all to make a few men rich. (Loud applause.) This month and the next month the , people entered into their inheritance, and it remained for the people from one end of the country to the other to decide whether the laws hereafter should be made for the benefit of a class or for the benefit of the nation. (Ap- plause.) Doubts had been expressed whether a govern- ment by the people for the people would be an honest government. He believed there would be a class of Liberals in the pew Parliament who would be determined that the laws should not only be honest laws but Christian laws. (Hear, hear.) If the Government was going to be honest, and there would be no fear of the Government doing dirty work, they would be able to recommend honestly and conscientiously that the State should buy the railways. Were all the railways in one hand and all worked with the object of giving as much accommodation to the people as possible, and at as low a price as possible, all passenger rates arid all rates for goods could be reduced by one half, and the State could get three per cent for its money. The traders of the country could then laugh at American competition and scorn the competition of Ger- many. Having referred to the improvement of the land laws in Ireland, the speaker advocated equal and jest laws for England and Ireland, and thought in all matters that concerned Ireland only,J Ireland should manage those Hear, hear.) He criticised the Conservative that country alone they bad proved themselves unfit to hold matters. Government ( in India, and contended that by their action in the reins of Government. (Applause.) He concluded by ridiculing the idea of returning to Protection. Isatisfaction the vigorous opening of the campaign of Mr. Mr. B. nuGH moved "That this meeting hails with .85 Gladstone in Midlothian, and hopes he will be returned at the head of a triumphant majority with Mr. Brunner amongst the number." (Applause.) Mr. Brea Bowe seconded the motion, which was sup- ported by Mr. B. KNIPETOS, in a vigorous speech. The resolution was carried With only three disaen-

RELIGION AND POLITICS. On Sunday evening, at Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, the Rev. T. Yonge discoursed on the subject, "The connection of religion with political aims and political contests." The reverend gentleman took as his text part of the 33rd v. of the 13th c. of St. Matthew, "The Kingdom of Heaven is like unto leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal till the whole was leavened." In the course of his remarks, Mr. Yonge said he should ' perhaps be told that it was a great mistake for a , minister to mix himself up in politics; that it was not his sphere and that he should confine himself to his spiritual duties. He was bound to say that that wee a doctrine to which he could not give assent even for a moment. He believed it to be a most grave mistake, and even to be fraught with serious dangers and con- sequences. Let them notice the idea upon which it seemed to be founded. It seemed to rest upon the notion that of all the realms of human life the realm of politics was the farthest away from religion, and therefore religious men, especially its teachers, should hold themselves as far aloof as possible from it. Now might not that be on the other hand a powerful reason why religious men and religions teachers should take up the matter of politics P For what was meant by politics? Were not politics the principles of government? Awd what could be more spiritually important than the principles upon which the nation , was to be governed, and what was the issue before the country at the present moment? That issue, broadly speaking, was the simple question of the best principles for the government of the empire. There was a question which went to the very root of the nation's honour and righteousness, and progress and prosperity. He said it was a question in which religion was supremely concerned, and a , question in which religious men, because they were religious men, ought to take their full personal share. A. minister might not be wise who should use his pal- pit as a place for displaying mere partisan zeal or at. tacking statesmen who may happen to be on the oppo- site side of politics to his own. But a minister was negligent of his ministerial duty who at a time like this should be silent to his people even on the Lord's day concerning the welfare of the nation and politi- cal duty. The politics of the nation would only be sound and righteous according as they were animated by principles which were derived from religion. "Righteousness," saith the old book, " exalteth a people." A nation's politics became religious in pro- portion as its politicians were religious men, and Christian men should be encouraged to throw them- selves into national affairs. Dealing with the politics of home affairs, Mr. Yonge said Christian men should seek to do everything they could to improve the con- dition of the people amongst whom they lived. The Christian religion was distinctly on the side of reform, ' and religious principles dictated the removal of bad laws and the provision of good ones. He need not tell them that, highly privileged as they were in this England of ours, still there were many social condi- tions amongst us which were directly opposed to the general welfare, and which hindered multitudes of people from advancing to prosperity and comfort. Religious men were bound to seek to procure legislation that would remedy existing evils. In his judgment Christian people should press very strenuously for laws whioh made for temper- ance reform. Of course they could not make a man sober any more than they could make him religious by Act of Parliament, but they could at any rate diminish his chances of intemperance by the regula- tion of that particular trade. At present there were needless opportunitics for drunkenness, and it was a Christian's duty to put temptation out of a man's way if it could be done. The Factory Acts needed extending to shops, and trams, and trains, for when men and women had to work twelve, fourteen. six- teen, and eighteen hours a day that was slavery, and it was endured to-day in free England. Re would not hesitate to say that religious principle dictated that political action should be taken in the question of the land. That seemed to be a question of the near future, and religion had a good deal more to say upon it than most people thought. If they viewed politics as they ought to be viewed, namely, as the means to secure right national government, and of promoting true national welfare, they became pre-eminently a sphere for the exertion of religious principle, and a Christian man ought Ito ally himself with whatever party in the state appeared to him from a study of its past history and its present policy to be aiming directly at the general good of the people.

SIR RICHARD. CROSS AND THE STEAD CASE. Sir,—That a few weeks will now see a great change In the sitting members, is a consummation as greatly to be wisiv.d as it is a certainty. The difficulties attending the pann- ing of the Criminal Law Amendment Act enabled people to know and note who were the opposers and obstructors by voting and amendments ef this most necessary r•form. Among others from whom we may hope to be freed are the present Home Secretary,. who spends publiiamonew and State influence in bringing to so-called justice &man who his worse detractors do not tax with a criminal motive. Neither party has reason to be proud of the action of their Home Secretary in regard to the evidence laid before the House relating to the cruel sin against young girls, but it was left to Sir Richard Cross and Judge Lopes to show how our English law can be used as a deterrent to the unmask-

lag of vice. Tnat the hard sentence under which Mr. Stead labours may yet further benefit the present and future generations, I look forward—if his health does not give way—to his using his powerful pen to create a public feeling that may induce the changing of our present law, which permits a ' judge to condemn to the same degree of punishment,and the hardship of coarse food, rough useless lahour, and solitary confinement, men or women who without caminal design have outstepped the law, and those provedly criminal in intention and act. Each day as these social questions come to the fore, I, as a woman, feel a more burning desire to have justice rendered to us, in enabling us to vote for men whose views of moral questions are of a higher standard thah that usually de- manded by men, who are often absorbed in purely political objects. As a woman also, I note with keen disapproval that more was made at the close of the Stead prosecution of the non-consent of the father to the going away of his daughter than of the fact that the mother had not provedly sold her daughter for vice. Until women are allowed their share in law making, this injustice of a one-sided parentship must be one of the anomalies under which they smart. In view of the circumstlance that only by pen and speech we can yet bring any weight.to bear on our representatives in regtrd to political events, I ask yon to publish my letter, to which I append my name.—l am, Sir, yours faithfully, S. FRANCES LATIMER. Glen View, Mannamead, Plymouth, Nov. 14, 1885.

BAND OF BOPE.—A magic lantern entertainment was given to the newly-formed Bind of Hope Society on Tues- day evening at the Warricgton-road Schools, by Mr. W. Pownall, with the aid of a dissolving view apparatus pre- sented by Miss Evans, Hurst-house. The views were of a most interesting character, and were much enjoyed. AN INTOXICATED SOLDIER.-At the Prescot Petty Ses- sions on Tuesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and A. R. Gladstone, William McDonne', attired in regimentals, was charged with being drunk in Eccleston-streel, Prescot, on the previous evening. The Prisoner promised not t 3 again get drunk during his furlough, and the Bench discharged him with a caution.'

MISCELLANEOUS Corrcggv.--On Tuesday eveninr an en- tertainment of a successful character took place in the new Assembly Hall, Kemble-street. The artistes were—Miss Dora Powell, MISS A. Gorse, Mr. George Barton (St. Helens), Mr. P. Richardson, Mr. D. Goldsworth ; violinlet, Mr. P. Lucas; pianist, Miss H. Quick: conductor, Mr. Jas. Berry; and a numerous glee party. The programme was of a high class. The proceeds were on behalf of Zion Chapel. . .
THE IRISH VOTE.

_ 1 Sir,—Much anxiety is being felt just new by the Tories, I as to how the Irish vo'e will go. No doubt the party who I have spent bye years in screaming out "Confiscation, Spoli- ation, and Robbery" would give a deal just now to be cer- tain of help from the Irish; yet it was these same Irish whom Lord 11. Churchill at Blackpool stigmatised as "Irish rebels," and celled upon Mr. Gladstone to "crush this legion of foul fiends." When we cast our eyes back and look over the past five years, we can but wonder at the im- pudence, nay, I may term it the inmtence of the Tories In presuming to look an Irishman in the face. Tbeir religion, their mud huts, everything an Irishman bolds dear, has been held up to ridicule, and yet to-day these Tories are hungering for place and power, and are anxiously hoping for the help of the Irish. The Irish have leaders, men who are dear to them, and men capable of advising them. One of them, Mr. T. P. i O'Conntm, speaking of the Tory party, says "They have dangled the bated figures of the Pope and the Church of I Rome before the people in the hope of working the demon I lof bigotry, ,' and by its means raisin themselves to power" - Irishmen, this is the opinion of Mr. O'Connor deliberately 1 given, and the whole histo;y of Ireland proves its truthful. ness. Where is the Tory that ever voted for Roman Catholic freedom? Where Is the Tory that ever voted ezainst coercion? Let Mr. O'Connor give the answer. He says :—"Suffice it to say, that to all the measures of reform which Mr. Gladstone intro- duced, and which entitles his Government to the credit of being the most beneficient Ministry ever known in our his- tory, the Tories were opposed." Barrett, 8.A., of Nor- wood, Liverpool. There were good congregarons. In the afternoon an address was given to the parents. teachers, and sob( ars of the Sunday school by Mr. A, E. A PHOTOGRAPHIC AGENT IN ,TROCBLE.—Before Messrs. W. L. Evans and A. it. Gladstone, at the Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a young man nam9d Robert Hannah, living at Liverpool, was charged on remand with obtaining by false pretences several small sums of money from vari- ous people at Wavertree. The prisoner had been employed by Mr. Blase, a photographer. at Liverpool, to canvass for photographs at 8s 6d and 12s 6d, but he had obtained orders for them at 68 61, though he bad had strict orders not to take orders at that price. When the orders were given the prisoner received a deposit on the amount. Su- perintendent Barker stated that the case was an intricate one and would occupy a considerable time in hearing. He was not prepared to go on with it that morning and ap- plied for a remand.—The prisoner was remanded until Saturday.

Irish tenantry relief out of this Irish^ Church /Ponds, Mr Chaplin. a Tory, moved an amendment comletrming the bill as" voting,public money for demoralizing objects'" but the Liberal Government carried it by 283 te• WEL Irishmen, remember-this next Tuesday :the Tories refused to grant money to help your landlord-ridden kin out of their troubles. They would rather it went intdthe bands ofmn alien church. Mr. Gladstone en the 25th of April, 1881, moved the second reeding of the Irieh Land Bill, This bill wee intended to protect the Irish tenantry against exhorbitant rents and un- just evictions Lord Elcho, a, Tory, moved, an amendment condemning the bill as "economically unsound, unjust, and impolitic.' The bill was carried by a majority of two to one; and yet when it came up for the third reading Lord Randolph Churchill persisted in again raising the debate. but was defeated by 220 to 1.• Irishmen are now asking for Home Rale. and English counties are asking for county government. Assuredly both will come in good time, yet hear what Lard Beacons- field said when speaking in the debate on the address in. 188dn—" The man who favoured such av dismemberment ci, the United kingdom was false to his. Sovoireign and his country." Mr. O'Connor, speaking of this." pious memory of the Tory party, says :—"Throughout his whole career his sole absorbing thought has been himself, and that to carry out his own advancement he has sacrificed every prisciple which men hold dear." Can Irishmen, after re thie,.and knowing as they must knows that Toryism is day what what it has always been, the insolent enemy of free- dom, the scornful scoffenot the dowa-trodelen—l aek,aeus Irishmen ever again look upon Toryism with favour? As Radicals in the pasta have kught and struggled for freedom, so they will in the future,, but they press upon Irishmen to do their duty and help in the good fight, There is great work yet to be done. Let Irishmen remember that it it. great landlords like Sir Gilbert: Greenall that refuse to have cottages erected on their estates, thus compelling poor Irishmen and Irishwomen to trudge scores of weary miles night and morning. Remember it is the Tories who insist upon making the poor Irish mother beg for her children's school wages; the Progressive party, to which Mr. W. Cros- field belongs, would save them from this humiliation. I was pleased to notice at Mr. O'Connor's meeting the large number of well dressed and happy looking young Irishmen. Let these remember that Warrington is now their hone, and that Englishmen and Irishmen, working together should have but one object, and that the creation of a happier future. CLIFFORD DIX. Nov. 18th, 1885.

A VIOLENT trALLWAT PUSENGER. -At the Borough Court, on Monday' a man named Ma* Jennings Was charged with beingdrunk and disor— derly on the platform of Bark Quay Station on the previOus night; he was also charged with smash- ing, two windows ,of a railway carriage, doing damage to they amount of 15s. Arthur, Harvey, a detective, in the employ a the Railway Company, informed the Ranch that on Sunday might his atten- tion was called to prisoner,who was in the carriage, of a train inicompany with some seafaring men. Prisoner was stripped, paced himself in a fighting attitude, and acted with great violence. Two win- dows of the carriage were broken, and prisoner was bleeding from the. hands and arms. Prisoner • denied haling broken the windows, and no evidence was proditced that he had done so. Prisoner was fined 10s and costs, or, in default, 14 days imprison-, ment.

WARRINGTON Di&TRICT HIGHWAY BOARD.—k meeting of this Board, was held at the offices, San- key-street, on Wednesday afternoon. The thair was taken by Mr. R. Houghton, and there were alSo present lifessrs..W. I'. Gooch, J. Hartley, and Cap, tam n Withington (ex-officio) ; Messrs. G. Lawton, B. Kerfoot, S. Marsh, _W. Royston, J. Houghton, J. Grounds, H. Woolf, Mr. White (clerk), and Mr. Thompson (surveyor):.—Sonie conversation took place with regard to the alleged encroachment at Lowton, andlt was. agreed ,pbat ,the question be fur- ther adjourbee—Mr. Kerfoot Called attention to the advertisement placards which were put upon the guide 'pbsts on the highways, and suggested that steps should be taken to prevent 'people putting' them there.,--, Captaln Withington thought it would be an improVemenf to have 'the posts repainted.— The Chairman said that was a bad time of the year ,to repaint them.--XaPtain Withington : Oh, yes, and besides it is electionlime, and one would hard= ISr know whether to paint them red or blue: (Laugh'- ter.)—lt was agreed, on the motion of Mr. Kerfoot, that steps be taken to prevent the guide posts be- In placarded, and the clerk was instructen to write to Mr. Bosco (Theatre of Varieties, ' Warrington), whose servants, It was stated, had put placards op. —On the suggestion of Mr. Royston, the surveyor was instructed'to make arrangements to remove a pinfold at Padgate;which it was stated had been complained of by the parishioners.—This was all the business of public interest. • THE BANKRUPTCY OF' Mu.'MOCIRE.--At the County Court, oh Monday, James Townend Moore, solicitors; came before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, to undergo his adjourned exemination in bankruptcy. It was stated on behalf of the trustee that he had exg- ambled the accounts, which had been, ,prepared by an accountant, but they were practically the same as those which had been previously filed. The bank- rupt had expressed 'his, utter inability to prepare the accounts, and he (the trustee) was prepared to ac- cept that statement ; at the same time he must call the attention of his Honour to the fact that the accounts did not satisfactorily explain the bankrupt's transactions.—The bankrupt, in answer to questions, said he had not kept any books this year, and was unable to give a better statement of his affairs than he had done.—The trustee said prao- tically the accounts did not advance the matter very much further, but he thought the bankrupt had,endeavoured as far as he could to prepare fur- ther accounts, but it unfortunately happened that he had no books or data to enable him to prepare the accounts He thought the bankrupt bad failed through sheer inability to file the accounts required, and he did not know whether his Honour would think it necessary to adjourn the examination again.—The bankrupt said if the trustee would give him any items he wanted an explanation upon he would endeavour to do all he could.—Mr. Worsley. (Deputy Official Receiver) said that the accounts preseated were practically of little or no value, and the bankrupt had expressed his utter inability to file a better statement of accounts. He (Mr.Worsley) was of opinion that the adjournments had only been the means of disclosing more errors and more inac- duracies, and he thought that they did not advance the matter at all.—His Honour said the examina- tion could not be closed, and from the opinion ex- pressed by the Official Receiver the examination must be adjourned sine die. —Mr. Percy Davies, who was present on behalf of a creditor, said the rent of the bankrupt's house at Newton had been paid by the trustee, therefore he did not propose to ask any further questions upon that.—The examination was then adjourned sine die • MR. T. P. O'CONNOR AT WARRINGTON.--On Tues- day evening an address was given by, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, in the National League' Orford-street. The chair was taken by Mn Lough- lin, president of the local Nationalists' League, and there was a good attendance.—The Chairman pro- posed a resolution pledging the Irishmen of War- rington to give their votes at the ensuing election ,as Mr. Parnell and the Executive of the Irish National League of Great Britain might advise.— This was seconded by Mr. John Mullins, after which Mr. T. P. O'Connor, who was received with loud ap- plause, addressed the meeting. He said they had come together as Irish Nationalists to discuss with each other the attitude they should take with regard to the coming election in that constituency. With re- gard to. Ireland itself he thought they might feel perfectly easy.' It was conceded on every hand that Mr. Parnell was bound after the general election to go to the House of Commons with an overwhelming malority of Irish electors, at his back. (Applause.) He would not undertake to give' them the exact number of Mr. Parnell's supporters, but he would be well within the mark when he said the number would be nearer 90 than 80. (Applause.) Mr. O'Connor then entered into an elaborate argument to prove that the Liberals were not better friends of Ireland than the Conservatives. Towards the end of his address he referred to the questions of Dia- establishment and Free Education. Mr. Chamber- lain's policy, he said, was bold, outspoken, and intelligible. "The Church was threatened, its funds were threatened, and Mr. Chamberlain guided the hungry eyes .of the secularists of this country to the, vast sums of money that were at the disposal of the Established Church, and he said "That is the place where we are going to get money for our free schools." That was seven or eight weeks ago, but now Mr. Glad- stone was saying in Mid-Lothian, "The Established Church; did I hear somebody speak of the Estab- lished Church? Why I never heard the Established Church uttered by anybody." (Laughter.) And Mr. Gladstone was innocent enough to think they were gullible 'enough to believe that Mr. Cham- berlain had not been talking about the Church at all, but about something in Siberia or some other part of the world. With regard to free schools he said, they would be free to the , Secularist, but dear to the Catholic and the Churchman. M. Chamber- lain meant that the School Board schools should have their doors open to all comers, and this system would end in beating down and annihilating the op- position of the Catholic, the Episcopalian and the Methodist Schools. He held that those 'who com- pelled a parent to send his children to a certain school were just as much guilty of persecution as those who would compel a man to go to a certain church. In conclusion be advised the Irish'electon of Warrington to vote according to the directions of Mr. Parnell. (Applause.)—The motion was then carried unanimously.—Mr. O'Malley (Liverpool) proposed a resolution in favour of Irish legislative independence. Mr. Gladstone, he said, of all the Liberal leaders, was most anxious to settle th,e Irish question. (Applause.) There could be no doubt aboutthat, but Mr. Gladstone desired many things; he desired the Land Act, but he only brought it in when Ireland was seething with revolution.—Mr. Cox seconded the motion, which was carried, the meeting soon after terminating. div.head: MR. BARLOW'S CANDIDATURE.
div.p: MR. BARLOW'S CANDIDATURE.
On Thursday evening a well-attended meeting ,of the supporters of Mr. J. E. Barlow, the Liberal can- didate for the Enutsfprd Division, was held in the _ _ .

Independent Methodisb.Chapel, Cbester-road, Grap. penhalt 'The chair was taitbn by Mr. W. Long, and amongst those present were Mr.. J. Et Barlow,. -Mr. A. ProYand, Mr. C. Broadbent, Rev. A. Ken- worthy, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Mr. W. Bradford, Mr. J. Thornley, Mr. T. Whitehead. • • Tee CHAIRMAN, in a few preliminary remarks, said that no reform in this country bad been carried except in the teeth or the strongest opposition the Tory party could baing,to gear. (Hear, bear.) They beard a good deal of the Tory working man, but for his part he could not upderstand what the new electors could hope to get by the ascendancy of the Tory party in the country. HP could not for Abe life of him understand it, the interests of the two seemed to him so entirely antagenistic. (Hear, bear.) He was glad of the opportunity of introducing to them a gentleman who had done them the honour of wishing to represent them in Parliament, a man who had' studied pllitieal questions well for himself, a man who was one of the people, and a man who if in Parliament would. be anxious to promote the best interests of the people. (Applause.) He asked them to remember that the Con- servative candidate, Mr. Abut Egerton. had or posed the Franchise Act on every occasion it was brought before Parliament when be was present. (A Voice: " That is true.") Could they in common honesty vote for a man who did his best to prevent them from hawing a vote? ;That was the question be would put to them He sensible men. (Hear, bear.) Having ridiculed the cry of the Church in daager, the chairman advised the new voters to take the matter of voting into their 'own bands,, and vote for the party they thought the best.' (Applause.) Mr. &Brow, who was received with cheers, referred to a cry which be understood had been heard in the neighbour- hood of Grappenball, that he was going to vote for the die. establishment of the Church. He would challenge anyone to look through his addresses since he became a candidate, and to find in them anything which would confirm the be- lief that he was prepared to vote for immediate diseatap. lishment and disendowment of the English Church. (Hear, hear.) In some parts of that constituency be was given to understand that pledges had been obtained of support to the Conservative candidate upon the plea that the Church was in danger, hut he thought he had shown them that so far as he was concerned that plea was one which was not accurate, and which existed only in the heated imagination excited partjsans. Mr. Barlow then read a letter he had received from Mr. J. H. Cooper, the hon. see, of the Church Defence Ashoelation, in answer to his (Mr. Barlow's) reply to certain questions as to disestahlishment and disendowment of the Church. In this letter Mr. Cooper thanked him for his aatistactory answer to the inquiry. Did they think it was exactly fair and straightforward of the supporters of the church throughout the division to say that he was go- ing to act in a way antagonistic to the church. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the ballet, he assured them it was per- fectly,secret and no one could possibly know how they voted if they kept their own mouths close. He also dealt , With certain questions which had been sent to him by the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, replies to which he sail they would probably see in the newspapers. The questions referred to the prevention of the importation of diseased cattle into this country; the relief of tie occupiers of land with regard to the rates ; the election of county boards ; railway charges, and the amendment of the Agricultural Holdings Act„and Mr. Barlow ,xoressed views favourable to the questioners in e,ch of these cue's. At the concl 051 )0 of his Boesch Mr. Barlow answered several questions to the evident setlefaction of the audience. I Mr. WHITEHEAD moved a resolution pledging the meeting to use every lawful means to secure Mr. Barlow's return by a large majority. He had, he said, heen engaged that day with Mr. Barlow in canvassing the voters of that district, and they had met with encouraging success. (Applause.) They bad met with some parties who declared they were going to vets' Tory, and he did not wonder at it, lowe Lase they bad no sort of reason to give why they were going to vote either way. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Some of them were going to vote Tory because their father vdted Tory, and one gentleman got ea far as to say he was goiog to vote They because his ancestors had done so, and be could trace them all tne way back to the ancient Britons. (Loud laughter.) He need not tell them that that gentleman's name is Smith. (Hear. hear, and laughter.) With regard to the Church he (Mr. Whitehead) thought that if Abe Tory party would set about reforming the Church disestablish- ment would probably be delayed almost indefinitely. If slabs@ reforms cfere made they would bear very little about disestablisbment for 50 years to come. (Hear, bear.) But if the leaders of the Church party wonld not make those reforms be took it.tbat the cry for disestablishment would gather force. (Hear, bear, and applause ) Mr. BRADFORD seconded, and Mr. PROVAND and Mr. C. BROADBRNT supported the resolution in an interesting speech, after which it was carried. only three hands being held up against It. It was stated amidst laughter that none of the three who voted against the proposal were voters.
Mr. BARLOW, in responding, moved a tote of thanks to the chairman. which was seconded by the Rev. A. KEN- WORTHY, and heartily accorded. The proceedings then ended.

There was a large attendance, and Brother George Clarke presided. Songs were Oven by Brothers Blinston and A. Seddon (of Ashton), John Taylor, K. Mac- kenzie, J. McDonald; a duet by Sistets E. and J. Clarke; recitations by Sister Lackland, Brothers' George B. War- burton, and J. Warburton ; readings by Brott.ers J. Barn- ard and George Makin, and an instructive address was given by Brother Morris Jones, D.E.S., of Liverpool, who, corn. melting on the ensuing Parliamentary eleelons, said he trusted the voters would exercise their rights according to their convictions. Years ago he consecrated his vote to the temperance cause, and he should continue to do to as long as the drink traffic existed. A vote of thanks was paid Brother Jones and the entertainers. on the motion of Brother John Taylor, seconded by Brother W. Dilitchell.

CONSERVATIVE MEETING IN WARRINGTON. , On Monday evening 0. Conservative meeting was held in St. .Paul's Schoolroora, Rolleston-street. The chair was occupied by Major Litton, who was supported on the platform by Mr. Whitley, M.P. (Liverpool), Aldermen Pickmere Davies, and Web- star; Rev. 6. Wilkinson, Captah;R'eynolds, Messrs. Carson, Mackie, R. Pierpoint,d., Pierpoint, T. Jolley, G. Greenail, and others. The Crtmaxerr said he was sorry to have to inform them that through suffering from a cold Sir Gilbert Greenall would not be there that night. His doctor, Mr. White, said it would be better if be remained quiet for a few days, after which he hoped to be again amongst them. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman then criticised the actions of the late govern. rnent, and alluding to their Egyptian policy, said they had caused the death of a large number of Arabs who were as brave fellows as ever stood in shoe leather. (Hear. hear, and laughter.) Mr. Causow said be had had a resolution placed in his hands which read as follows :—" That this meeting pledges itself to use all legal and just means "—be asked them to mark that 4 legal and just moans "—(hear, bear.)—and he wondered whether the other side would propose such a reso- lution—" to return Sir Gilbert Greenall as tile representa- tive for Warrington.at the coming election, he having ever shown himself to be a consistent Conservative, and having on all occasions manifested a deep interest in all that con- cerned the prosperity of Warrington." There had, Mr. Carson mid, been a qu.stion raised about the polling day in War- rington. One would have thought that was a very simple matter about which there could be no differences of opinion, yet simple as it seemed the Tories could not do right even in that. ' He himself was very much in favour of Tuesday for the polling day. (Hear, hear.) Referring to White Cross works, be said that within the walls ef that works there was no politics. (Applause.) A man had ample time under the Act of Parliament to record his vote, but if over and above that any man wanted to devote himself to the in- terest of his party on the election day, they would strain a point to let him go but if it interfered with the conduct of their business could it be expected that they would let him go ? (Hear, hear.) Dr. MACKIE, in seconding the proposal, referred at some ength to his own experience in electioneering matters in fighting the Montrose burghs. He said he had promised to give his working-men friends an evening's entertainment after the election on Scotch " heckling." Mr. WnorLev, M.P., who was received with applause. supported the proposal. Since be had .formed his connect Sion with the public life, and with the interests of the grea- constituency he represented, he had arrived at the conclu- sion that it was a very great mistake to address the work. ing classes, or any other class, in the language of patronage, or even in these days of enlightmeat to give specious and False promises. Whatever his position in life might be, a man should speak honestly from honest convictions. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to the expenditure during the last year of the late Government, he }said it was the largest that had taken place since the battle of Waterloo, and although he was not born then, some of his friends on the platform might leave been. (Laughter.) With regard to Mr. Chamberlain's lend proposals, he said he wondered whether Mr. Chamberlain recollected that the semi thing Was tried in the time of Louis XIV. (Laughter.) He should like Mr- Chamberlain to look at what happened then. (Hear, hear, and laughter.; Mr. Whitley aleo eondemned free edu- cation, and said that if unsectarian education was to be given to the children at their schools, then he had no faith whatever in the future greatness of -this country. (Ap- plause.) The resolution was then carried unanimously. - Mr. R. Pisepoisr "proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Whitley, which was seconded lay Mr. JOLLBY, and carried. Mr. Wrnausv, in responding, referred to the statement that he bad made that Mr. Chamberlain's money was not Invested In England. Mr. Chamberlain, he said, had accused him of making that statement without foureiation. As to that, he could only say that he spoke from inforiciai- tion conveyed to him but if Mr.Chanaberlain had written ti him to say that that statement was without foundation, he would have accepted his word and withdrawn the charge. But he (Mr. Whitley) remembered that in IMO be ventured to say that Mr. Bright had opposed the extension of the Factory. Acts, and vet Mr. Bright wrote that "Mr. Whitley told lies as all the Tories do." (Laughter.) In conclusion, referring to Sir Gilbert Greenall, he said that though be might be advanced in years, he (Mr. Whitley) would give him the best help he could to represent the interests of this borough. (Applause.) He also proposed a vote ot thanks to the chairman. Alderman PICIOIERE, in sepono.ling the proposal, said he was glad the Conservatives had gained the day so far as the fixing of the day of election was concerned. lear, hear.) Whea he was Mayor the Liberals always wanted to push the day of electien further on so that they might have a little more time. But ha was always very firm on that point, and looked to the Town Clerk and the good of the town. He always fixed the day as he liked, and as tioiy liked. (Applause.) Captain REYNOLDS supported the proposal, which was carried, and tha meeting Ora ended.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICR PAR- I LIADIENTARY DIVISION OF MIESHIRE. GENTLEMEN,—I ask for your votes as the chosen Caed(date of the freely-elected Association of the Liberal party in this Division. My faithfulness to Liberal principles is, I trust, suffisiently ateeeted by long years of work and sacrifice in the. Liberal cause, and by m v life as a c.tizen in your ml Ist. To all who are acquainted with the facts relating to the sub' sidence of the ground in the Salt district and familiar with the laws made for the p•omotion of the public health, it is clear that these laws are in some respects unsuitable to your circum- stances, and it will be my constant care to see that this excep- tional district shall have fair play. The loss to owners and te• ants and public authorities through the rising of brine ought to be made good to them, and nn brine raised ought to be allowed to escape payment of its share of this loss. The arrangement made more than a century an 1 a half ago wbeu there was practically no subsidence, that the surp'us funds of the Weaver Trust should be paid over to the comity is now and has long been a crying injustice, and I hope for the support of all fair-minded men in my efforts to bring it to an end. The trades in our district are largely dependent upon a foreign demand, and lam urged pith by personal interests and by my free-trade principles to endeavour to enlarge and to Stimulate that demand. For your sake and for the sake of the natives of India, I shall advocate a large reduction in the enormous tax levied upon salt entering that country. This tax of over five pounds per ton is both a folly and a crime. 4. polit clan can hardly have a higher aim set before him than the attainment of free-traue in talc and Alkali, the first a necessary of life, and the sec ind an ab,olute requirement of el elite Olen. The Liberal party has, after lone years of work, succeeded in giviirg to all classes a share in the government of the cern- try. The work of the Government will h-nceforth naturally be directed to securing the good of all clas,es. I firmy bel've it will befound thet this work will hurt no class, for or un- just privilege injures those who posses it, no less than those who possess %not. LINV-MARING. I would give to the majority in the House of Comm( ns full power to regulate its business so as to prevent the waste of public time, arid I would allow to no mart the right to sit In the House • f Lords sole'y on account of his birth, but would reserve that privilege absolutely for rneo woo had earned t he respect of their fellows • THE OWNERSHIP AND OCCUPATION OF LAND AND BUILDINGS. By preventing the creation of life interests, I would make each owner of laud a free man, free to sell and tree to let By compelling the registry of such tree owner:hip I would make the baying and selling of land shnple and cheap. This I would do with the object of largely increasing the number of freehelders and especially the number of men Heine in their own houses. By the abolition of the law of distraint, I would do away w.th a system under which the tenant is always compelled to I sacrifice far more than the landlord is entitled to receive, and other creditors of the tenant are placed at an unfair disadvan- tage—a system by which men and women are rendered thrift- less and unhappy, end by which paupers are made. Whilst I would not have the law permit a tenant to injure his lendierd's proper. y, I would allow no landlord to confis- cate his tenant's property at the end of a tenancy-whether of a houseplot. a salt works, or a farm—simply because it is at- tached to the freehold. Any bargain to the contrary should be void in law, as opposed to public policy. A GRICULTURE. For the manufacture ot food, the greatest trade in the coun- try, special enactments are necessary. Wtetet securing the landlord from injury, I would prohibit restrictiors being put upon the farmers' freedom of sa e and eultivation, being firmly convinced that they know their JWII bus.nets best, and that if the farmers prosper every other class in the community will be bettered Security of tenure to the farmer is also a necessity fe• the good of all, for the reason that without it there many opera- tions which require much time are hindered. I symp. tithe strongly with the just and increasing dernaud foi• some power of appeal against untair rents, and Indulr rail- way rates. VIE DEPRESSION OF TR 9.DE. The unlocking of the land will increase our hatvest s. Tne'eurrinshieernent of leaseholds will stimulate all trades connected with building Country and town alike thus benefitted, our home trade will again prosper. • The abelition of all eostoms duties (except those on alcoholic liquors) would greatly eepaud our foreign trade. Afeasures such as these which make for freedom are the true remerdes. To tie men's hands ha the bonds of a restric- tive tariff is not ties way to pr-mote the prosperity of a, natiou. LOCAL GOVERNMENT. Our present system Is sadly wasteful and ye y I,seffietent. We have too many local authorities, too many rates, and too many rate collectors. We want a village board, a district board, an i a county beard, invested with large powers, all worklug in concert, and all elected by ballot, cacti ratepayer to have one vote. All rates should be levied upon one demand note, and should be paee.ble half by the owner and half by tee tenant. Thns we should have both equally interes ed, and each edu- cating himself for the mauageteent of national sffams by his share in the management of local affairs. All r. property. Inch] .log rights of way, illegally dividuals dining the last 00 years, I w ota" - -id put it under the charge of the 10c.._ To local public authorities power should be given to take land at a fair price for all public purposes, and amongst those purposes aught to be included allotments for working- men. Upon an active mun'clpal life, in town and errantry alike, depends Ira tbe main the solution of the great problem of the housing of the poor. ' _

HELENS, ON THURSDAY, 261 rt NOVEMBER, 1885, In aid of the Puns of the WEST LANCASHIRE MASONIC CHARITIES, Under the distinguished patronage of HIS WORSHIP THE MAY9R OF ST.
